Latest Update: The Benefits of Biking for Seniors, Including the Mental and Physical Payoffs

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2064 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • We know you think we’re going to tell you all the ways cycling improves your heart health and muscle strength—and it does, but guess what?
  • In fact, even though many people associate aging with physical and mental declines, regular exercise—like a daily bike ride—can help slow or even reverse some of these effects.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

We know you think we’re going to tell you all the ways cycling improves your heart health and muscle strength—and it does, but guess what? According to a 2023 scoping review in Frontiers in Sports and Active Living, studies show that when older adults cycle regularly, their happiness improves and they are better able to maintain their quality of life.

In fact, even though many people associate aging with physical and mental declines, regular exercise—like a daily bike ride—can help slow or even reverse some of these effects.

Read More of Ride Strong at 50+.

According to recent reports, “Regular physical activity helps seniors maintain good health, improve their quality of life, and increase their overall well-being,” Mary Sabat, MS, RDN, a personal trainer and dietitian in Georgia tells Bicycling. “It can enhance physical strength, flexibility, and endurance, making it easier to perform daily activities and maintain independence.”.

Those are just few reasons why biking for seniors is so great—but here are all the advantages you gain when you start pedaling regularly.

Sources indicate that while almost forms of physical activity improve physical and mental health, cycling is particularly well-suited for those in their golden years due to its accessibility. After all, cycling is easy on the joints, even for those with joint pain or injuries. “It can be tailored to individual fitness levels and adjusted to accommodate different abilities and physical limitations, too,” claims Sabat. “Recumbent bikes, trikes, or electric-assist bicycles can be used to make cycling more accessible for those with mobility challenges or balance problems.”.

Robert Patterson, a cyclist and lawyer, has been cycling for more than 40 years. He points out all the obvious aerobic and strength-building gains he’s enjoyed over the years, but also the psychological benefits. “Cycling also benefits my mental health. My attitude and overall focus are always improved by being on the bike,” he states.

Here are nine reasons, according to the experts, for you to saddle up and hit the road (or the gym) for a ride.

Aerobic exercise is the key to managing heart health. Because the heart is a muscle, it needs to be exercised on a regular basis to maintain its strength and optimal function. And because the heart and lungs work together with the venous system to deliver oxygenated blood to your muscles, any exercise that increases your heart rate and breath rate for an extended period of time will help improve your heart health and overall cardiovascular function.

Plus, as anyone who has ever pushed the pedals and pumped through a 20- or 30-minute bike ride knows, cycling will definitely get your heart rate up. The repetitive cycling motion qualifies as a moderate to intense form of aerobic exercise that you can easily adapt to your personal fitness level. This means that even if you haven’t exercised in years, by starting at a lower intensity and making adjustments to your workouts based on your heart rate, you can safely and effectively add cycling to your weekly routine.

It has been revealed that “As individuals age, the risk of heart disease increases,” says Sabat. “Cycling is a low-impact aerobic exercise that helps improve cardiovascular fitness, strengthens the heart muscle, and enhances blood circulation. It can lower the risk of heart attacks, strokes, and high blood pressure, thereby promoting a healthy heart.”.

In fact, a series of two 2019 review studies (part 1 and part 2) published in the British Journal of Sports Medicine found that all forms of cycling reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease and also reduced the risk factor profile for poor heart health—meaning that cyclists had better body composition stats, blood lipid profiles, cardiorespiratory fitness levels, and more time spent exercising. All of these together help mitigate the risk for developing heart disease.

You can combat practically any chronic condition, including heart disease, along with type 2 diabetes, arthritis, and cancer with a regular ride. Exercise helps keep the blood flowing, systems moving, and cells turning over in a way that promotes overall health. For instance, high-intensity exercise (and high-intensity cycling, specifically) helps improve blood glucose response, according to research, which may reduce the risk of type 2 diabetes.

Even in the case of cancer, participating in a regular cycling routine has been shown to reduce the risk. For example, May 2020 study published in The Lancet found an association between participating in a daily bike commute and a 16 percent decrease in cancer mortality and an 11 percent decrease in cancer incidence.

According to recent reports, “By incorporating a ride here and there into their routine, seniors can reduce the risk of chronic conditions. These conditions can be debilitating, but with regular exercise, seniors can take proactive steps toward prevention and management,” Josh Weight, a certified sports physiotherapist and the director of Gravity Physio in Australia tells Bicycling.

It’s not unusual for seniors to experience regular joint pain associated with arthritis or previous injuries. In fact, according to the National Poll on Healthy Aging, about 70 percent of older adults report current joint pain. This can be exacerbated by extended periods spent sitting, or simply not moving around much, as sedentary behavior is directly associated with increased incidences of knee and other joint pain.

While on the surface this may not seem like a massive deal, it can lead to a cascading series of events where joint pain or arthritis contributes to a reduced range of motion. This reduced range of motion can influence balance, coordination, and even the ability to perform everyday tasks. These complications can also contribute to a reduced quality of life and even an increased risk of falls. As such, any activity that can be done without contributing to joint pain while protecting and strengthening the structures that help stabilize the joints (muscles, tendons, and ligaments) is an crucial undertaking for older adults’ overall health and well-being.

Sources indicate that “Cycling is a low-impact activity that puts minimal stress on the joints, making it an excellent option for individuals with joint-related issues. It provides a cardiovascular workout without placing excessive strain on the knees, hips, or ankles,” Sabat says.

Whether done on an indoor bike or a more traditional road or mountain bike, one thing’s for sure: Cycling works the legs. It takes muscular strength, power, and endurance to keep the pedals moving, especially when climbing a hill or ramping up the resistance. But it’s not just the legs and glutes that benefit—cycling can help build strength in the shoulders, upper back, and core, as well.

Of course, you may not be looking to build massive quads as one of your long-term fitness goals, but developing muscular strength isn’t just about looking strong—it’s about maintaining your quality of life.

Research estimates muscle mass begins to decline by 3 to 8 percent every decade following your 30th birthday, with those rates increasing further once you hit 60. This age-related muscular decline over time makes it more challenging to continue doing everyday activities like climbing stairs or carrying groceries. It’s important to participate in exercises, like cycling, that will help maintain or build muscle mass over time to safeguard your ability to perform these daily activities.

In fact, according to a 2015 review study published in the European Review of Aging and Physical Activity, adults over 70 years of age experienced increased muscular strength and power when participating in a cycling exercise program at least three times a week for 12 to 16 weeks. This data flies in the face of anyone who believes they can’t develop muscle or strength as they age—it’s not only possible, it’s critical to overall health and functional ability.

It has been revealed that one area in which cycling can be particularly beneficial is balance and coordination. This has ties to muscular strength, as strong, trained muscles tend to perform and react more quickly to stimuli than those that aren’t worked regularly. However, it also has to do with the unique requirements of cycling itself.

“Cycling requires balance and coordination to stay upright and navigate,” states Andrew White, a personal trainer and owner of Garage Gym Pro. “This can be especially beneficial for seniors as these abilities tend to decline with age, increasing the risk of falls and injuries.”.

Recent findings suggest that this isn’t just conjecture—a 2018 prospective study published in the Journal of Aging and Physical Activity found that older adults (between the ages of 65 and 85) who cycled daily had better balance, a faster pace while walking, and better self-reported lower-extremity function compared to those who didn’t bike regularly. Based on this study, it appears that cycling helps preserve balance and coordination which contributes to lower-body function that can help prevent falls.

Just as muscle mass tends to decline with age, an associated change in body composition takes place, which often leads to increased weight gain. And as weight creeps up, so do the risks for heart disease and chronic illness, particularly in populations considered obese.

Industry observers note that cycling and other forms of exercise can help keep weight and other disease risk factors in check. This is partly due to the muscle-protective benefits exercise offers, but also due to the increased calorie burn that occurs during moderate- to high-intensity exercise like cycling.

“Cycling can help seniors maintain a healthy body weight, reduce excess body fat, and prevent obesity-related health challenges,” Sabat emphasizes.

Industry observers note that it’s not unusual for seniors to experience social isolation that can contribute to physical and mental health decline. Changes in health, mobility, or driving status can keep seniors alone at home. This is unfortunate because strong social connections are positively associated with longevity.

Sources indicate that cycling can provide seniors with an accessible way to get out and about, and to also engage with other people of all ages. “Cycling can be an enjoyable and social activity for seniors. Exploring outdoor trails, participating in group rides, or engaging in community cycling events can foster a sense of camaraderie and connection with others,” indicates Weight.

And for seniors who want to start cycling, but don’t know how, community cycling clubs offer a great way to learn and connect at the same time.

In addition to the benefits of social interaction, cycling can boost mental health in a number of ways, especially if you’re riding your bike outside. “Cycling outdoors provides an opportunity to connect with nature, which can be therapeutic and stress-relieving,” claims White.

In fact, according to a 2022 study published in the Journal of Affective Disorders, individuals who participated in outdoor cycling (or other outdoor activities like walking, jogging, or team sports), were less likely to experience depression than those who were inactive. Likewise, there’s evidence that even a single outdoor exercise session (like cycling) can impact mood, more than indoor exercise equivalents.

Sources indicate that even in the absence of an outdoor setting, physical activity as a whole is good for mental health. “Regular exercise releases endorphins which can elevate mood and reduce symptoms of anxiety and depression,” Sabat explains.

One final benefit of cycling for seniors: It can support cognitive function. “Studies have shown that physical activity can have positive effects on cognition and may help reduce the risk of cognitive decline and dementia in older adults. Exercise promotes better blood flow to the brain, stimulates the release of hormones that support brain health, and improves memory and attention,” Sabat shares.

Industry News: The Anti-Movement Core Routine Every Runner Needs

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that glute bridge post-run.
  • Sources indicate that for this article, physical therapist Jennie Hansen analyzed a newly introduced study on anti-movement vs.
  • “Core strengthening” is a term runners frequently toss around.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that glute bridge post-run. (Photo: Aleksandr Kondratov, Getty).

Sources indicate that for this article, physical therapist Jennie Hansen analyzed a newly introduced study on anti-movement vs. dynamic core training and built a simple, science-backed core routine for runners based on the findings. The routine targets the deep stabilizing muscles that protect your spine and improve performance.

“Core strengthening” is a term runners frequently toss around. We all know we need it. But what exactly is it, and what should it entail? (Hint: Not crunches.).

When we talk about the core, we mean the abdominal muscles, low back, gluteal, pelvic, and hip muscles that support the spine and trunk. These muscles include both smaller, deep groups that attach directly to the spine to provide stabilization and larger, more global ones that can assist with stability and produce movement.

Recent findings suggest that why do we need this area to be strong? Well, even non-runners need to pay attention to their core strength to avoid lower back pain, which is the top cause of years lived with disability. Athletically, the core must create proximal stability to allow for powerful, efficient movements distally—which requires adequate strength combined with coordinated neuromuscular activation and control. So, core strength is certainly important for pain reduction, injury prevention, and athletic performance.

It has been revealed that when running, the trunk serves to provide a stable base of support so that the legs can effectively generate the forces that create forward movement. These forces are transferred across the trunk and counterbalanced by the arms, requiring coordination between the hips, trunk muscles, and shoulders.

According to recent reports, while running appears to be purely a forward (sagittal plane) activity, the trunk muscles are hard at work controlling side-to-side (frontal plane) and rotational (transverse plane) forces. Muscle activation and timing change with speed, with higher speeds generally requiring more control and work. The deep trunk muscles also contribute to respiration.

In a recent development, while some small trunk motion naturally occurs with running, excessive motion is detrimental. Increased trunk flexion is associated with decreased running economy and increased loading rates and vertical impact forces. Increased lateral trunk lean has also been linked to increased loading rates, which may play a role in the development of certain injuries.

Recent findings suggest that even though most of us know that crunches are out, there’s still plenty of confusion about how to train our cores. While strength work doesn’t need to look exactly like running, it does need to meet (and exceed) its demands—meaning that stability should be emphasized over motion.

Enter a recent study comparing neuromuscular activation between “anti-movement” and “dynamic” core training. Unlike traditional dynamic core exercises, which work the trunk and spinal musculature by moving through flexion, extension, rotation, and side bending, anti-movement exercises resist external forces, forcing stabilization throughout the trunk—basically, trunk isometrics.

The 12-week study compared a combination of Pallof holds and plank variations (incorporating bands and the TRX suspension trainer for progression) in the anti-movement program against a dynamic program that included exercises such as sit-ups, leg raises, jack knives, Russian twists, windshield wipers, and back extensions (incorporating Swiss balls for progression).

While both exercise groups demonstrated enhancements in neuromuscular efficiency compared to a control group, improvements were overall greater in the anti-movement group, particularly within the deep local musculature that activates prior to limb movement and plays an notable role in stabilizing the spine.

The authors therefore hypothesized that this enhanced neuromuscular efficiency could improve endurance, delay fatigue, and reduce the need for recruitment of larger, more global muscles—thus protecting the spine and potentially decreasing injury risk while improving performance.

Runners can apply these findings and consider an “anti-movement”-focused core routine, similar to the one used in the study. Nothing fancy or extensive is required—just one exercise each to resist the trunk’s motions (flexion, extension, rotation, and side-bending/lateral flexion). Simple plank variations and other holds work well to streamline your core routine efficiently and effectively.

Targets: Anti-extension · full core (local and global).

The front plank is a classic core stability exercise that falls into the anti-extension category, challenging most of both the local and global core muscles.

Targets: Anti-flexion · spinal extensors and glutes.

While the study used a supine plank as its anti-flexion exercise, the shoulder position required could be a limiter, so bridge holds are likely a more practical way for many runners to work the posterior trunk muscles, including the spinal extensors and gluteals.

Targets: Anti-lateral flexion · lateral trunk and hip muscles.

The side plank can be considered an anti-lateral-flexion exercise, challenging the lateral trunk and hip musculature.

Targets: Anti-rotation · obliques and deep abdominal rotators.

The Pallof press is a common anti-rotation exercise, challenging the deep abdominal rotators, including the obliques.

  • In a recent development, this walk takes on different forms depending on your specific circumstances.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Photo: Getty Images; oleh_slobodeniuk).

According to recent reports, the last two months of the year are crammed with holiday traditions. Some are sweet and nostalgic, others revolve around food and drink, and most require some amount of socializing.

But there’s one unsung custom that deserves a moment of praise, or at least a little quiet appreciation. It combines some of the simplest mindfulness practices, gets you outdoors, and helps ensure all of the other traditions can unfold a touch more seamlessly.

I’m talking about the holiday walk.

In a recent development, this walk takes on different forms depending on your specific circumstances. It might provide some one-on-one time with a friend or relative you don’t see often. (You can make it the stereotypical “cousin walk” of your youth.) Maybe it’s an opportunity to walk any and all dogs also hanging out in the house. The holiday walk could also, appealingly, be a solo endeavor, a chance to step away from any obligations or unwelcome conversations and catch your breath.

Sometimes it’s an actual hike or a long, slow meandering down a nearby trail. Most of the time, though, it’s a simple stroll around the block.

At its core, the holiday walk is about escaping the revelry for a beat of peace and quiet. It’s a change of pace that lets you return to your specific gathering with more appreciation and less stress and social overwhelm. And it can be one of the most gratifying ways to cultivate presence…even if it means needing to excuse yourself for a short while.

It’s also a chance to hone a number of other mindfulness practices that you can take back with you to the celebration and can make your seasonal experience a more pleasant one.

According to recent reports, walking alone is proven to reduce feelings of stress and anxiety while boosting mental and physical health. Try including one or all of the following to make your amble even more intentional.

In a recent development, getting any amount of fresh air is always a win, but adding some purpose to your inhalations and exhalations through breathing exercises can help you get the most out of your holiday walk. Try simply lengthening your exhalations, matching the beat of your inhalations and exhalations (and the spaces in between) with box breathing, or letting it all out with lion’s breath.

If you’re struggling to access feelings of gratitude (for whatever reason) this season, try turning your appreciation toward your body. Pay attention to the way your feet, legs, and core carry you; how your lungs want to breathe deeply; and how cool it is that you have this vehicle that lets you move through the world.

Another means of cultivating micro-gratitude, glimmers are just about noticing beauty and joy around you. Fallen leaves (both their color and the way they crunch underfoot), passing clouds, someone’s laugh, a cool rock, notes from a familiar song that are audible from a passing car…glimmers are everywhere. When you get back to your gathering, notice them there, too.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Do you ever feel like you’re stuck at the starting line?​ ​ You want to improve your health and fitness. But there’s so. much. going. on.

It has been revealed that every time you try to make a plan, you get 1,000 opinions on the “perfect” workout. The “perfect” diet. The “perfect” routine.

You’re not sure where to start or what to do.

I hear this story so often that I gave it a name. And a face. 😅.

(h/t to Leo, our awesome illustrator who makes these images for us from scratch! 🙌 ) ​ Meet Major Overload.

He’s every fitness voice on the internet at once.

In a recent development, do this. Never do that. Fasted cardio. Never fasted cardio. Carbs are fine. Carbs are the enemy.

The Major loves it when you have 100 tabs open on your browser, but haven’t done a workout yet.

It has been revealed that he wants to keep you plugged in to The Matrix. He feeds off of you staying stuck in planning mode while he drains your batteries.

My client Eric ran into him a few months ago.

He’d spent weeks searching for “best at-home workouts to lose fat”. ​ In his words:.

It’s the way I felt when I tasked myself with running Nerd Fitness’s Instagram.

According to recent reports, A million different opinions on how to do it. Hours spent researching. And weeks later, I still hadn’t filmed an actual video yet. 😅.

I was firmly stuck in analysis paralysis.

Recent findings suggest that same boss battle as Eric. Different rabbit hole.

What got me unstuck was the same thing that helped Eric.

It wasn’t finding the “perfect” strategy or plan.

1) Follow one proposal and block out everything else for now.​ ​ ​2) Commit to taking some small action, most days of the week.

The first one turned Major Overload’s volume down.

Recent findings suggest that I didn’t need every voice. I needed a simple starting point. One that didn’t have a gajillion hoops to jump through.

The second one is where the learning actually happened.

I didn’t have to be perfect. I had to commit to imperfect reps.

I’ve learned more from a couple of weeks of posting than from all the agonizing I did beforehand.

Here’s what I told Eric, and what I’d tell you, too:.

Recent findings suggest that unless you’re Doctor Strange, scrubbing through 14 million possible futures to find the one where everything works out, you can’t know what perfect looks like. Neither can I. Nor anyone on the internet, no matter how loud they get.

Luckily, you don’t need a perfect blueprint.

Enough structure to get out there and do the thing. Not so convoluted that you never get started.

That’s why we built the Beginner Bodyweight Workout and our Strength Training Templates.

So you stop getting stuck at the starting line, and start putting in the reps.

Moving from planning to action does two things at once.

It breaks the inertia, and it teaches you what fits in YOUR life.

And that’s where the real magic happens.

It’s where you learn that, actually, training later in the evening works better for you than trying to force yourself up at 5AM.

It’s how you discover that splitting your workout up into two 15-minute chunks works better for your schedule.

Or that you prefer training with weights to training with bands.

You won’t know those things until you get out there and try.

It’s just as key to learn what DOESN’T work for you as what does.

Three weeks of taking imperfect action will tell you more about what works for you than three months of listening to Major Overload ever could.

Instead of searching for the “perfect” proposal, build your action plan.

1 or 2 actions you can take this week, small enough to test and see how they feel.

That’s exactly what we did with Eric. ​ We mapped out his first few action steps. Things that fit his life, and he felt confident doing.

Sources indicate that and now? He’s 4-months in and training consistently. Not perfectly. Consistently.

And that’s made all the difference for him. 💪.

Sources indicate that one more thing about Eric’s story I want to leave you with. He also shared this with me as part of our conversation:.

In a recent development, that’s something else I hear all the time. And it’s nothing to be ashamed of!

Sometimes, the bravest thing you can do is to ask for help when you need it.

That’s the whole reason we’re here.

When you’re stuck at step one, overwhelmed by information and not sure what’s worth your time, that’s exactly where a coach can help.

Our Editors Ride-Tested Virginia Tech’s Top-Rated Road and Gravel Helmets—Including a $60 Pick That Punches Way Above Its Price

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • Recent findings suggest that as a cyclist for over three decades, I’ve crashed many times.
  • It has been revealed that when shopping for upcoming road and gravel helmets, cyclists often base their choices almost entirely on looks, price, and overall comfort.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Recent findings suggest that as a cyclist for over three decades, I’ve crashed many times. Unfortunately, I’ve also had a few concussions. Because of this, safety is important to me when I choose a new helmet. Over the last few seasons, I’ve tested dozens of great helmets, from budget picks under $50 to go-fast aero lids and lightweight models for over $500. Plus, I also test trail helmets, commuter lids, and everything in between.

It has been revealed that when shopping for upcoming road and gravel helmets, cyclists often base their choices almost entirely on looks, price, and overall comfort. Depending on our riding goals and budget, we also balance weight, aerodynamics, and style. We want safety features, but many riders assume most helmets do a decent job of protecting our noggin—they’re all certified, right?

Helmet safety isn’t as straightforward as it may seem. Current Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) standards—as well as more rigorous, voluntary requirements, such as those from ASTM—account for straight-line impacts and G-forces from a collision. These standards don’t address the rotational forces from a crash that contribute significantly to concussions and traumatic brain injuries. Plus, the CPSC’s standards took effect on March 10, 1999—advancements in technology, design, materials, and manufacturing over the last 27 years have changed bike helmets.

According to recent reports, so, what standards and certifications cover rotational forces? Currently, none. To better protect against rotational forces and reduce concussions, many brands incorporate Mips liners (and similar anti-rotational designs) into their helmets. Brands also test their helmets internally to their own, generally unpublished, criteria. The Virginia Tech helmet lab’s STAR score provides the best independent testing and ranking for helmets across most cycling disciplines.

Industry observers note that virginia Tech tests helmets for safety; it doesn’t evaluate fit, comfort, weight, price, or overall practicality. Bicycling’s test team collectively rides tens of thousands of miles each year on tarmac, gravel roads, singletrack, and commuting. That means we have a lot of time to ride-test lids—including more than half of Virginia Tech’s 5-STAR-rated road helmets.

For 15 years, Virginia Tech has tested helmets through a battery of 24 impact tests that analyse safety performance and assign an overall STAR (Summation of Tests for the Analysis of Risk) score.

It has been revealed that “The overall score estimates the number of concussions the average person would see if they experienced identical impacts at rates matching their weightings while cycling,” indicates Virginia Tech’s lab. The lower the STAR score, the better a helmet performed in testing.

Then, to each helmet it tests, Virginia Tech awards an overall STAR rating (one through five); helmets with four- and five-STARs are “recommended.” The lab does not recommend helmets scoring three STARs or fewer.

It has been revealed that virginia Tech has tested and published results on more than 300 bicycle helmets. To date, the lab has awarded 56 helmets its coveted 5-STAR rating, and another 104 received 4 STARs. To make researching and choosing a upcoming helmet easier, it also sorts the helmets it tests into mountain, road, urban, multi-sport, full-face, and E-bike categories. Of the 5-STAR helmets, 21 of them are road lids.

Editor’s Note: These helmets are the top 5-rated road bike helmets in Virginia Tech’s bicycle helmet rankings as of November 9, 2026. The Virginia Tech helmet lab regularly tests helmets and updates the overall rankings; the top 5 can change at any time. Please consult Virginia Tech’s bicycle helmet ranking list for up-to-date rankings.

According to recent reports, “Who is Pikio?” and “What is a Si Oblik?” Those were the questions our editors all asked when we saw this helmet rocket to the top of Virginia Tech’s STAR ratings. The Pikio isn’t only the top-rated road helmet; it’s also Virginia Tech’s best-performing helmet, period. It beats the others by a considerable margin, logging an unbelievably low 4.61 STAR score. For context, the difference between the Pikio and the second-place overall Canyon Deflectr RLS mountain bike helmet is 2.21 points; that’s the same gap between the 2nd and 28th positions in current rankings.

Recent findings suggest that all of that safety comes at a relatively steep $379 cost. While the Si Oblik’s price aligns with other range-topping helmets from Giro, POC, Specialized, and MET, Pikio’s looks and finish feel comparable to mid-tier models from more well-known brands. For example, Pikio’s color options are somewhat conservative choices, and the rear strap anchor point is through-shell.

It has been revealed that the Si Oblik fits well and has a broad range of adjustment for my medium-sized head. The rear adjusts up and down (to account for head shape and hairstyles) and features a dial to microadjust fit. The straps, however, are not as cleanly executed as expected for the price, especially compared to POC or Specialized, and I found them slightly tedious to adjust. On road and gravel rides, the Si Oblik’s airflow doesn’t feel bad, but I didn’t test this lid in peak summer heat. And while the Pikio weighs about the same as Giro and MET helmets in this test, it feels physically bigger, though not as mushroomy as the POC Cytal.

In a recent development, for a fresh brand, Pikio Labs made a solid first effort. Unlike its competitors, Pikio doesn’t have decades of trial and error or a flashy WorldTour team. Hopefully, as the company grows, it can dial in details, sharpen pricing, and spice up the aesthetic, because the Si Oblik already sets a very high bar for safety.

The POC Cytal’s unique shape and bold look make it easy to spot in a peloton. Another reason the Cytal stands out is due to its overall size—it’s a physically substantial lid. But despite its dimensions and slightly heavy weight, it doesn’t feel that large on your head while riding and ventilates surprisingly well.

The Cytal’s great ventilation comes from its massive vents and internal air channels that funnel air directly over your forehead while riding. I found out how well it vents while riding over the summer in France during “la canicule” (the heatwave). I could still feel the Cytal pushing air in 100-degree temps, even if it was roasting hot.

Industry observers note that in our recent review of P2R’s $100 aero-helmet, ride tester Tom Messina stated it “has no business being this good.” And with its lower price and STAR score, we say the same thing about P2R’s $60 A20 Mips. With its excellent safety rating, great adjustability, and budget-friendly price, the A20 Mips outperforms many helmets that cost three, four, or even five times its price.

It has been revealed that P2R somehow hits the A20’s low price without cutting corners on features. It has nice straps with adjustable quick clamps that offer plenty of adjustment. P2R also includes a USB-rechargeable light that magnetically clips into the rear vent for commuting or extra visibility on the road.

The one downside we found with the A20 Mips is that it feels optimized for rounder head shapes. While it fits me well, a couple of others who tried it on stated it was a little snug near their temples.

Recent findings suggest that given the Trenta 3K Carbon’s pedigree, it’s hard not to name it “Best for Racing.” UAE Team Emirates’ official sponsor is MET, and the Trenta is one of the helmets it supplies to the squad—including Tour de France champion Tadej Pogačar and World Champion Brandon McNulty. While UAE riders often race the Italian brand’s Manta aero helmet, they sometimes pick the lightweight, well-ventilated Trenta 3K Carbon for climbing stages and training.

Industry observers note that unlike some modern helmets with similarly strong protection, the Trenta feels light and racey on your head, and almost disappears when you’re riding. The straps offer good adjustability, and the Mips Air Node liner protects without feeling bulky. However, the Trenta’s biggest drawback is its price tag. At over $500, this is an expensive piece of kit.

Ranked 14th overall and 5th in road helmets, Giro’s Aries Spherical stands out in our testing for its overall comfort, adjustability, low weight, and great looks. While its STAR score is much higher than the first-place Pikio, the Aries is a very safe helmet and received Virginia Tech’s 5-STAR rating. Having crashed on the road while wearing an Aries Spherical, I also know this helmet works.

Of the approximately one dozen road and gravel helmets in my rotation at any given time, I reach for the Aries Spherical most often. The Aries fits my head perfectly, and the Roc Loc dial system offers plenty of adjustability for hair length or if I’m wearing a cap underneath in rain or cold weather. Giro makes the Aries in a wide range of colors and graphics to fit almost any rider’s personality or fashion.

It has been revealed that as Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and Latest England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

How to Hold Yourself Accountable Without Beating Yourself Up

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Here’s what that looks like inside real coaching conversations.
  • When most people picture “accountability,” they picture a drill sergeant.
  • Someone standing over you going “What were you thinking?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Here’s what that looks like inside real coaching conversations.

When most people picture “accountability,” they picture a drill sergeant.

Someone standing over you going “What were you thinking? Why did you skip that? Do you even want this?“.

(And if there’s no drill sergeant handy, we do a pretty good job of beating ourselves up all on our own.).

Here’s the thing: if being hard on yourself worked, it would have worked by now.

Great accountability isn’t built on being a hard-ass.

It’s built on forward momentum and honest feedback.

Industry observers note that the drill sergeant questions YOU. Your motivation. How much you want it.

Real accountability helps you try again quickly.

Then helps you see what you’re doing well and what can improve.

Sources indicate that A client of mine had a hectic week. Travel, out of their routine, workouts missed.

The drill sergeant move is “why didn’t you do your workouts?!” at the exact moment they were already struggling.

Sources indicate that “Hey! I know this has been a hectic week. Let’s do some push-ups together. Do a set next chance you get and shoot me a 👍. I’ll do one too.”.

This got a 👍 and a “Thanks for the encouragement! This week has been so hectic my schedule got away from me.”.

That win got them back on the routine.

Then we build off of that by looking ahead to the next few days.

“How’s the rest of this week looking for strength training? I went ahead and put together a few variations in case you’re short on time.”.

When you’re already struggling, the question isn’t “hey, why didn’t you do that?”.

It’s getting the next available win.

Then looking ahead to what’s coming up after that.

But forward momentum is only the first part of the equation.

The second step is giving honest feedback on both the wins AND the challenges.

To be a neutral observer. To point out what’s going well, what’s not, and suggest how we can improve it moving forward.

Based on the actual human in front of me: their unique goals, motivations, and whatever flavor of chaos they have going on in their own life (work, family, travel, illness, injury, etc.).

“Hey! I reviewed the strength workout on Friday. Solid work all around here. I can see from your form check video that you’re doing a better job staying balanced across your whole foot on the squat. 💪.

In a recent development, I also noticed that the middle of the week has been tougher to get consistent workouts in. You’ve hit 2 out of the last 4 midweek workouts. I know work has been crazy with the project deadline you have coming up, so my guess is you’re getting buried and it makes it hard to get to the gym. Am I on the right track? I have some ideas for how we tackle that next week that I’ll drop down below in a video for you.”.

This is the honest part. It didn’t go anywhere!

But instead of berating you for missing a workout, the goal is to look at all the evidence and suggest next steps.

Sources indicate that including if the evidence states that something SIGNIFICANT needs to change. It’s all on the table.

Accountability isn’t punishment for what you didn’t do.

It’s helping you decide what you do next.

If your week went haywire, before you beat yourself up, take this approach:.

This is one piece of how our coaches do accountability. Here are a few more ideas for you:.

#194359. Tech Report: The beliefs these Master Health Coaches had to unlearn (and you might too)

Tech Report: The beliefs these Master Health Coaches had to unlearn (and you might too)

📅 28 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3092 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Precisionnutrition

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For example, in Motivational Interviewing, an effective communication style used in coaching and counseling, there is something called the “righting reflex.”.
  • The righting reflex is the instinct to help or “fix” a client, as well as give them directions on how best to change.
  • Sounds like a great instinct to follow if you’re a coach, right?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For example, in Motivational Interviewing, an effective communication style used in coaching and counseling, there is something called the “righting reflex.”.

The righting reflex is the instinct to help or “fix” a client, as well as give them directions on how best to change. Often, the righting reflex is particularly strong in people who really, really care.

Sounds like a great instinct to follow if you’re a coach, right?

We are now entering upside-down-land.

Motivational Interviewing describes how this (beautiful, well-intentioned) instinct to help can actually hinder a client’s progress.

That’s because when we swoop in to fix, correct, or steer, clients often do the exact opposite of what we’re hoping for: They dig in and get defensive.

Push someone the “right” way and, paradoxically, they’ll start advocating for the very habits they came to you to change. You end up being the one arguing for change—which leaves them to argue against it. Everyone walks away a little more frustrated, and the client feels more stuck than ever.

Instead, great, experienced coaches learn to get curious instead of corrective. (They might even encourage the client to explore not changing!).

It has been revealed that that’s just one example of an upside-down skill that separates a good coach from a masterful one. But it’s certainly not the only example.

We asked some of Precision Nutrition’s most seasoned PN Level 2 Master Health Coach Certified coaches a simple question:.

What’s something you were sure about early in your career that you later had to unlearn?

Their (honest, and sometimes humbling) answers are below, plus the wiser way forward they adopted, and are now sharing with you.

Our first lesson to unlearn comes from PN in-house coach Jeremy Fernandes, PN2-MHC.

Sources indicate that with over 14 years of coaching experience, Coach Jeremy is known for his friendly, comfortable, “talk to me like I’m your buddy” coaching style. Which is ironic, because as you’ll see, he started off his career leaning heavily on a rigid structure that was actually pushing clients away.

Here’s what Coach Jeremy has to say:.

Sources indicate that at the beginning of my career, when I’d been a personal trainer for a year or two, I had a friend ask if I offered nutrition coaching. And my first move was: Here are all of the forms. And when I say “all of the forms,” I mean all of them—I probably sent this person 20 pages to fill out.

Three weeks later I had to hunt them down, and we ended up filling them out together—which took two and a half grueling hours.

If not for those forms, we could have started actually coaching, like, 20 days earlier.

Industry observers note that not long after, another friend revealed up at my door with this white-hot intensity: “Tell me what to do, I’m ready,” they stated. And I immediately dumped a metaphorical bucket of ice water on them with those darn forms. It was radio silence after that.

The problem was that I was operating like my sole job was to extract information from a person and then solve the mystery—as if I had some advanced pattern recognition about you that you didn’t have about yourself.

And unfortunately, I kept on that terrible path for a while.

What finally prompted a change was going through the Level 2 Master Health Coaching Certification.

Going through that course, I saw there was a better framework—one that doesn’t rely on me robotically extracting information.

I learned to let the client take the lead, and then just listen and maybe ask a few good questions. And it works so much better—for everyone.

It has been revealed that now I work from the assumption that my client knows themselves better than anyone. One of my most valuable questions is simply:.

“What have you tried before, what did you like about it, and what didn’t you like?”.

When I let people take the floor, they nail the really big stuff more often than not—in a way my paperwork and my detective work never facilitated.

Honestly, the forms were me projecting professionalism, because back then I didn’t feel like a professional. My identity as a coach never felt natural until after L2. Now, just letting someone talk feels like coaching. We start with a connection, and then I just let them fill in the gaps.

The next lesson to unlearn comes from PN Director of Community Engagement and in-house coach Kate Solovieva, PN2-MHC.

With over 16 years of coaching experience, Coach Kate is known for her honesty and incisiveness. She has a way of dropping realness on her clients that may first feel like a shock, but ultimately ends up getting her clients to the heart of the matter much faster. But one hard truth she had to face was her own.

Here’s what Coach Kate has to say:.

Sources indicate that you know the story: You reach the healthy weight, the habits lock in, and the weight just stays stable on its own. You hit “save” and move on with your happily ever after.

And that is not the case at all.

At least most of the time. It’s true, some goals really are like that. If you want to run a marathon, you can pick a race date, follow a training program, show up to the start line, run it—and then you never have to run again and you will still have achieved that goal. That’s a real destination; you cross the finish line once and check the goal off.

According to recent reports, but weight loss, muscle gain, body recomposition, building a habit of movement or eating well—those aren’t like that. Especially when the goal means working against a chronic tendency, like a predisposition to high blood pressure, or to hating exercise, or to living in a larger body than you’d prefer.

Those goals come with a pretty good amount of ongoing and intentional maintenance—daily, weekly, monthly. There’s no save button.

According to recent reports, this realization didn’t come from one single client or one moment for me. It came through a collection of observations, including observations of myself. But once I saw it, it changed how I coach.

I realized that if there’s no real finish line, then my job is to manufacture finish lines along the way. That way, my clients continually feel like they’re accomplishing something satisfying.

I take the big goal and break it into something specific and daily—and then I insert smaller outcome goals into the journey.

For instance, someone going from sedentary to wanting to lose 100 pounds is facing a huge goal, full of behaviors and identities they’ll have to grow into. So along the way, we might set a goal of running a single mile without stopping. Strictly speaking, that doesn’t have much to do with the bigger goal—but it also has everything to do with it. It’s checkable. Achievable. Ideally it’s also something they’re a little excited about: fun, interesting, maybe even a little scary, but still within reach.

Because here’s the thing: It’s very hard to motivate the human brain to work out three times a week for the rest of their life to “get healthier.” “Being healthy” isn’t tangible, it’s not immediate—you can’t feel that far-off outcome in your body.

It has been revealed that but striving towards a fun, achievable goal in the next three to six months? That’s real. It also builds in structure, and provides those little spikes of motivation—the hit of dopamine you get from working hard at something and actually accomplishing it.

Health isn’t something we ever fully “accomplish” or check off. So we have to give ourselves these little concrete goals along the way that we can feel and see and be delighted by.

The next lesson to unlearn comes from PN content creator Azul Corajoria, CPT, PN2-MHC.

With over nine years of coaching experience, Coach Azul’s coaching fingerprint is empathetic, relatable, and endlessly encouraging.

While these traits always came naturally to her, for a long time, she thought she had to adopt an opposite style to help certain clients (and herself) to “get back in line” when habits didn’t go as planned.

Here’s what Coach Azul has to say:.

Early in my coaching career, I thought that if someone wasn’t following through on what they mentioned they would do, it’s because they needed more structure or just to get their “head in the game.”.

I couldn’t understand why someone would invest in coaching and then not do the things we planned.

It was especially confusing because most of my clients had “discipline.” They were successful, responsible, hardworking people who highlighted up for their jobs, families, and everyone else in their lives.

Meanwhile, I was also “disciplined” in many areas of my life—yet I also struggled with eating well and exercising consistently.

According to recent reports, at this time, I felt this lack of consistency was my fault, and went straight to being really angry at myself. I thought I was just missing the “perfect something” (the perfect workout, the perfect diet) to help me change, so I’d just move from thing to thing, but each one would bring fresh disappointment.

I was incredibly frustrated by this cycle, and my response was to get stricter and harsher with myself.

It has been revealed that it’s hard to say when it all changed. It wasn’t an overnight epiphany; it was a culmination of years of getting curious, being open to different methods, like the Body Positivity Movement and Intuitive Eating. I dove into self-compassion and positive psychology research, and I went through the PN Level 2 Master Health Coaching Certification.

Recent findings suggest that I applied everything I learned, and I noticed that the more open and curious I was, the better my clients responded. Slowly, that turned into the realization that the more open and curious I was with myself, the better I would respond.

Industry observers note that I stopped binge eating. I started enjoying exercise more. I took more career risks.

Sources indicate that I learned that when we can respond to a setback with curiosity instead of punishment, we’re much more likely to stay engaged. When I allow myself to be disappointed by an action, take responsibility for it, and remain on my own side, I feel safer reflecting and taking risks. The more I do that, the more likely I am to achieve the things I want.

Sometimes the most helpful thing we can teach a client (and ourselves) is not how to push harder or “just be more disciplined.” It’s how to make a mistake, remain on our own side, and keep going.

Because self-compassion is not the opposite of accountability; it’s often what makes accountability possible. (I call it “compassionate accountability.”).

It has been revealed that none of us will ever be the “perfect” coach, and we don’t have to be. The more human I’ve allowed myself to be, the better relationships I’ve had with my clients. My biggest goal as a coach is to create an environment my client feels safe to come back to with not only their wins, but their losses. The safer they feel being honest and open with me, the safer they’ll feel to try latest things—and over time they’ll build the confidence to do it themselves.

The next lesson to unlearn comes from PN in-house coach and Level 2 Master Health Coaching Certification instructor Dom Matteo, PN2-MHC, NBC-HWC.

It has been revealed that with over 16 years of coaching experience, Coach Dom stands out for his non-judgemental attitude and excellent listening skills. For Dom, these traits are relatively inherent, but they’ve also been carefully developed and honed, in part by letting go of what he calls the “coach’s ego”—the assumption that he already knew what a client’s success should look like, and that he was the one who got to keep score.

Here’s what Coach Dom has to say:.

I took that stated goal at face value, and treated whatever number they gave me as the measuring stick, as the most notable thing to work towards.

But then, I’d see a client struggling to do their actions even 50 percent of the time, and I’d think: ‘This person is never going to be happy, because this won’t get them to the goal weight they told me they wanted.’.

Remember, I assumed the number was the real goal.

However, again and again, those same clients would turn out to be genuinely happy with their progress, not because they hit their exact goal, but because they felt so much better about themselves and their lives.

What I learned is that the stated outcome was almost never the true goal for many of them. When they mentioned ‘lose 50 pounds,’ what they really meant was: I want to feel better. And being consistent even half the time, over a year, netted results they were thrilled with. Because they felt better. They felt different.

In a recent development, so the thing I had to let go of was my own scorecard. Who am I to tell a client that what they’re doing isn’t good enough, if they’re happy with how things are going?

My latest definition of progress became less about approaching a specific final number and more about another question: “Am I a little better today than I was yesterday?”.

These days, I spend time up front helping a client build what we call a “wellness vision.” We clarify their values, and what success actually looks and feels like to them.

Then, instead of assuming I know how to measure their progress, I’ll ask: “How will you know if this is helping? How do you want to measure success?”.

Industry observers note that the result is that even a client who’s fixated on the scale can see other signs of progress long before the scale actually changes. And often, those other signs are the things they really wanted to change in the first place.

It turns out the most useful thing I can provide isn’t a judgement about whether a client is succeeding. Instead, it’s to help them determine and notice their own success, by their own measures.

The next lesson to unlearn comes from PN in-house coach and Level 2 Master Health Coaching Certification instructor Jason Bonn, PN2-MHC, NBC-HWC.

Recent findings suggest that with over 18 years of coaching experience, Coach Jason’s clients describe him as patient, observant, and deeply dedicated. He has a knack for spotting a client’s potential—though as you’ll read in this story, Coach Jason learned that getting too focused on a specific version of that potential sometimes kept him from seeing other ways his clients could grow and thrive.

Here’s what Coach Jason has to say:.

For me, progress felt like a puzzle to solve: I’d play with adjustments to exercise volume or intensity, calorie or protein intake, eating more slowly, eating to 80 percent fullness, all the fundamental stuff.

But then, because of one client I still think about, I began to shift how I thought about “progress.”.

It has been revealed that he was in our PN coaching program. He lost 40 to 50 pounds in his first six months—which was great—but then everything stalled.

It has been revealed that we tried adjustment after adjustment for the next two and a half years. We added more protein, more cardio, and worked through his particular peccadillo, eating corn chips at night. But none of it moved his numbers.

What got me was that he kept showing up anyway: three straight years, re-enrolling each time, even though the scale had plateaued.

That told me something was working for him—it just wasn’t something I recognized yet.

According to recent reports, in his third year, we stopped looking only at the gym and his diet, and started looking at his whole life. He was a landscape painter, so we built his practices around that instead: make a sketch or work on a painting daily, anything that sparked some joy or interest. Within a couple of weeks, he was getting on his bike and riding out to further places for different scenery to paint.

In part because of this client, I’m now a lot more cognizant of coaching the whole person, and considering their Deep Health. Weight and performance numbers are just one piece of a much bigger picture that includes relationships, emotional wellbeing, and what someone finds meaningful.

I’ve also stopped zeroing in on “problem” behavior.

I try to understand a person’s life overall—not just the behavior I’ve been hired to help with—because there’s a connectedness to it all, and behavior tends to emerge within the context of someone’s life.

I’ve also stopped treating the coaching relationship as a means to an outcome and started treating it as the main thing—the sun that everything orbits, the glue that holds it all together.

That client kept coming back for three years because the relationship mattered to him. By the end, I’d stopped thinking I was failing him. The weight loss was such a small part of the success. The relationship was the bigger piece.

Coaching mastery isn’t about stockpiling more information. (Your clients can Google information or ask a chatbot, and so can you.).

It’s about developing the judgment to know when to use what you know, when to set it aside, and when the most helpful thing you can do is nothing at all, except be there.

But that kind of judgment is hard to build alone; it takes practice, expert feedback, and a few humbling moments with real clients—which is exactly what the PN Level 2 Master Health Coach Certification is designed to offer.

With enough practice, self-awareness, and the right training, you can gain the wisdom and skill of the above coaches.

But the best coaches, it turns out, are defined less by what they know than by what they’ve been willing to unlearn.

Ready to move from competent to truly masterful—in 20 weeks?

The PN Level 2 Master Health Coaching Certification is an advanced, practice-based program designed for coaches who want to work at a deeper level—and do it sooner than the traditional 5–10 year path.

This is not a nutrition course.

It’s a mentored, small-group experience that prepares you to:.

You’ll learn directly from PN’s most experienced coaches through weekly live mentorship, structured self-study, and real-world coaching practice.

Level 2 is NBHWC-approved, making graduates eligible for:.

These credentials expand your career options and set you apart in an increasingly crowded field.

Tech Report: Is Your Cycling Computer Lying to You?

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1293 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that spend enough time comparing power meters, and you’ll quickly learn that they don’t always agree.
  • If you use a power meter for training, what matters most is that the numbers you’re seeing today are comparable to the ones you saw last week or last month.
  • According to recent reports, but what if your power meter isn’t the only thing affecting those numbers?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that spend enough time comparing power meters, and you’ll quickly learn that they don’t always agree. Put a power meter on your crank and another on your pedals, and the numbers may not match exactly. That can be frustrating when you’re trying to figure out which one is right, but for most riders, a small, consistent difference isn’t necessarily a problem.

If you use a power meter for training, what matters most is that the numbers you’re seeing today are comparable to the ones you saw last week or last month. Whether your threshold is actually 250 watts or 255 watts matters less than knowing that an interval at that power represents the same effort from one ride to the next.

According to recent reports, but what if your power meter isn’t the only thing affecting those numbers? What if the bike computer recording your ride is changing the data before you ever upload it to Strava or TrainingPeaks?

Sources indicate that I recently noticed something odd while testing a cycling computer. At first, I was doing this to compare GPS track accuracy, but since I was testing, I also paired all the devices to my heart rate strap and Quarq power meter. When I compared the ride files afterward, what stood out was that their power numbers didn’t match. Initially, the differences were small enough. But when I looked more closely, I noticed it immediately. Every time I stopped pedaling, one computer still recorded power.

Before I get into what the heck sticky watts are, I should say I first learned about the concern in 2025 when I saw a video from Shane Miller, who goes by GPLama on YouTube. The video is called “Power Meter Data Recording: The Wild West?”, and it’s worth watching. Shane was the first person I saw digging into this particular recording issue with cycling computers.

So what the heck is it? Sticky watts happen when a cycling computer keeps recording a power value for a few seconds after you’ve stopped pedaling. Instead of dropping to zero, the last power number gets “stuck” in your ride file until the computer finally catches up.

Industry observers note that let’s say you’re riding along at 250 watts and stop pedaling as you approach a corner. Your computer might continue recording 250 watts for a few seconds while you’re coasting. On a graph, that can look like a flat line extending beyond the point where the power should have dropped.

Industry observers note that A few seconds might not sound like much, but think about how often you stop pedaling on a typical ride. Every corner, descent, stop sign, or moment spent coasting in the group is another opportunity for those extra watts to show up in your file. And if you stop pedaling after a hard effort, the computer could be holding a much higher number than 250 watts, which can skew your data.

Recent findings suggest that it’s also worth distinguishing this from the setting on some computers that lets you exclude zeroes when calculating average power. That setting changes how an average is calculated. Sticky watts affect the power values recorded in the ride file itself, so those extra values can still be there when you upload the ride for analysis.

On one ride, I compared the DURA 2 with a Garmin Edge 850 and an Edge 1060. The two Garmins recorded almost identical power numbers, but the DURA 2 consistently came out higher. When I looked more closely at the files, I found repeated instances where the COROS continued recording the last power value after both Garmins had dropped to zero.

Industry observers note that the difference was especially noticeable during a series of short, hard efforts. After one effort, the DURA 2 recorded 565 watts for four seconds while both Garmins recorded zero. After another, it held 656 watts for three seconds. Across a roughly three-minute section containing several of these efforts, the Garmins averaged about 260 watts, while the COROS recorded nearly 307 watts.

Those short efforts make the issue easy to see, but the difference indicated up across the ride, too. In the roughly 98 minutes of matched power data I compared, the DURA 2 averaged about 186 watts, while both Garmins averaged about 179 watts.

According to recent reports, on a second ride, I compared the DURA 2 with a Hammerhead Karoo, Wahoo ELEMNT ACE, and Garmin Edge 850. Again, the COROS recorded higher power through a section with several hard efforts followed by coasting. The Garmin recorded lower numbers than the Karoo and Wahoo in that section, which reminds us that differences can go both ways when computers record the same power meter.

I was honestly surprised to see this on the DURA 2. The original DURA had similar problems early on, but its power recording improved with subsequent updates, and it performed well in GPLama’s 2025 video presenting the issue. I don’t want to turn this into a story about picking on COROS. The firm has a good history of updating and improving its products, and I expect it can address this issue on the DURA 2 as well. For now, these files show why it’s worth paying attention to what your cycling computer records, even when you trust your power meter.

Sources indicate that if you mostly ride for fun and don’t pay much attention to your power data afterward, a few extra watts in your ride file probably won’t change your life. But if you use that data to track your training, compare rides, and work with a coach, those differences can matter.

The significant problem is that sticky watts don’t necessarily add the same amount to every ride. A steady climb with little coasting might show no difference. But a ride with lots of corners, stop signs, descents, or short, hard efforts followed by coasting could produce a much larger one. That makes it harder to compare rides or judge how much work you actually did.

The easiest way to check is to record the same ride on two cycling computers paired to the same power meter. You don’t necessarily need to buy a second computer. If a friend has one you can borrow, pair both to your power meter and record a ride with a few clear transitions from pedaling to coasting.

It has been revealed that alternatively, you can look closely at the power files your head unit generates. Do a couple of hard efforts, like sprints, where you stop pedaling at the end, then zoom in on those sections. Look for a flat section where one computer continues recording the same power value for several seconds after the other has dropped to zero.

And yes, I know that I’m definitely in some deep weeds over here, and it can be tough to argue that a cycling computer recording a few extra watts is a huge problem worth tackling. For many riders, it might not matter at all. But the current crop of cycling computers is also the most expensive we’ve ever seen. These devices are marketed and sold as precision training tools, and accurate data recording is central to that. These devices should do that, and riders shouldn’t have to question it.

Test Editor Dan Chabanov got his start in cycling as a Upcoming York City bike messenger but quickly found his way into road and cyclocross racing, competing in professional cyclocross races from 2009 to 2019 and winning a Master’s National Championship title in 2018. Prior to joining Bicycling in 2021, Dan worked as part of the race organization for the Red Hook Crit, as a coach with EnduranceWERX, as well as a freelance writer and photographer.

#194357. Bored With Your Workout? Try a New Level, Not a New Program

📖 Baca

Bored With Your Workout? Try a New Level, Not a New Program

📅 25 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (540 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nerdfitness

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When we dug into it, here’s the pattern that emerged:.
  • Strength training, then running, then a yoga challenge, then back to lifting with a different app.
  • Nerd Fitness Coaching was the latest in a long line of fresh starts.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Here’s the client story this comes from.

This was the first thing a new client said to me.

When we dug into it, here’s the pattern that emerged:.

-> See something latest, give that a try.

Strength training, then running, then a yoga challenge, then back to lifting with a different app.

Nerd Fitness Coaching was the latest in a long line of fresh starts.

And here’s the thing: all of it was GOOD.

She was moving. She was trying new things. She was having fun (at least at first).

But she was frustrated with herself.

She felt like she kept starting over and never getting anywhere.

And she wanted help figuring out what to do.

Let’s be real: trying something new is exciting.

Industry observers note that A fresh program, a new class, a new challenge. There’s a buzz to it.

Sources indicate that and that buzz isn’t bad. Enjoying it is a big part of what keeps people moving.

The catch is that most goals need some repetition.

In a recent development, getting stronger, running farther, learning a skill. You get better at the things you practice again and again.

So the question isn’t “how do I stop getting bored?”.

It’s “how do I keep some of that new-thing fun AND repeat things enough to see progress?” 🧐.

That’s what we worked on together.

When I built her program, I kept its overall shape the same week to week.

But inside it, a few key exercises got a target. Something like:.

“Once you can do 12 reps with 25 pounds, we level up.”.

The targets were far enough away to stretch her, and close enough that she could hit them in 2 to 6 weeks of focused practice.

In a recent development, when she hit one, we leveled up that exercise: upcoming reps or weight, or a new variation. Everything else stayed put.

So something was always changing.

There was always a target she was closing in on and a level she’d recently beaten.

Recent findings suggest that but the frame stayed the same. We were still working on the same overall qualities.

And that’s what let her progress stack up instead of resetting every few weeks.

She was able to stay really consistent with her program.

Industry observers note that she still fell off some. (Life happens.).

But when she came back, she wasn’t looking for something new.

She was excited to pick up her program and keep progressing.

And sure, sometimes her goals would change.

We spent 6 months training for her first half marathon, then switched gears to focus on building muscle.

But that was a choice, not a restart.

If you love bouncing between things and you’re happy doing it, keep bouncing.

This is for when the bouncing starts to feel frustrating.

Before you reach for a latest program, try a new level.

✅ Set a target you could reach in 2 to 6 weeks (a rep count or a weight).

✅ When you hit it, level up that one exercise with new reps, a new weight, or a new variation. Leave everything else alone.

It has been revealed that I’m excited to see what you come up with. 😃.

#194355. Triathlon as the Latest Run Club: Community Without “Bro Culture”

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 15m • 📚 Deep Dive (2949 w)
