Triathlon as the Latest Run Club: Community Without “Bro Culture”

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2949 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Triathlete

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Triathlon club founders and disruptors share how they are building inclusive communities.
  • What do you do when you’re fed up with the elitism that can lurk in various pockets of triathlon?
  • From free 140.6-mile races and no-drop rides to psychic readings and book clubs (and more book clubs), meet the tri club disruptors who are daring to shake up triathlon by prioritizing inclusion, whole health, and social connection over watts, body exclusivity, and snobbery.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Triathlon club founders and disruptors share how they are building inclusive communities. (Photo: Courtesy Alexa and Branden Scheel, Corinne Geerdts Merten and Melissa Niemuth-Seamonson, Hannah Bradbury, Hilary Topper, and Kyla Lupo).

What do you do when you’re fed up with the elitism that can lurk in various pockets of triathlon? You could throw up your hands in defeat and frustration over the bro culture and inclusion challenges, vowing to train in solitude like a spandex-clad, multisport monk. Or … you could start your own tri club, team, group ride, or clinic.

From free 140.6-mile races and no-drop rides to psychic readings and book clubs (and more book clubs), meet the tri club disruptors who are daring to shake up triathlon by prioritizing inclusion, whole health, and social connection over watts, body exclusivity, and snobbery.

When Altitude Multisport Club, a tri club in Denver, Colorado, was founded in 2010, the board consisted of all men.

Industry observers note that “While friendly, it had a very ‘bro’ vibe and club events were rarely organized by leadership and club meetings were salesy,” notes Erin Trail, Altitude Multisport Club’s former president and current volunteer. “What did it for me was a no-drop group ride that the current president and coaching director were on. I had done three Ironman races, and they dropped ME. I knew the route and was fine, but I thought: ‘What if I was a newly introduced person? What kind of experience would this be?’”.

Since the president was term-limited, Trail was able to step up as president in 2016 to change the atmosphere to a friendlier, more inclusive one.

“That first year was very hard. I decided to make the club more inclusive and friendly to beginners and women, eliminating sales or conflict of interest issues and improving communications,” Trail states. “I lost a LOT of club friends because I wanted to make things different. Half my board quit because they didn’t want to be held accountable. But in my first year as president, membership grew from 50 to 150 members!”.

Today, Altitude Multisport Club features winter Sunday pool swims with a coach and travel camps to Moab and a local state park in addition to regular training and racing activities.

“My second term as president was much better, with a diverse board that I handpicked. We added a family membership so households, including kids, could join at a group rate,” Trail claims. “And we made it clear that the environment is welcoming, organized, and a safe space to learn for everyone.”.

“A LOT of skinny white men. That’s what I saw in triathlon. I didn’t see enough women, and I really didn’t see anyone who was bigger. I realized that if I wanted to see more folks that looked like me, I had to be the coach that made triathlon a place for all folks, regardless of size, shape, color, or anything else,” claims Kyla Lupo, who took things into her own hands, getting certified as a coach, learning everything she could, and starting her team, Go Big!, with just one athlete and “a bunch of friends pretending to be my team.” Since then, Go Big! has grown to 22 athletes.

“Our team makes a point to let folks know that they are already loved, exactly as they are. Team Go Massive! stands for a radical level of body inclusivity, both in sport and the world,” Kyla says. “On Team Go Big!, we work to overcome our fear and doubts while getting fit and ready for the start line. Anyone can tri in the body they have right now.”.

Social connection is crucial to the Go Massive! community and takes the form of weekly team meetings where members from around the country learn, share their goals, ask for support, and expect accountability.

It has been revealed that “We are from all over the country, but there’s a Tuesday morning virtual trainer ride to further connect us. And of course we get to party together at races,” Lupo says.

Disruptors: Alexa and Branden Scheel.

Recent findings suggest that people often join tri clubs to find community, only to discover that they are a small fish in a big sea. When you’re one of hundreds of athletes, you and your journey can get lost in the mix.

Sources indicate that “My husband, Branden, and I were part of two different teams like that. We felt like ‘just another membership,’” Alexa Scheel says.

According to recent reports, so she and Branden pursued certifications from USA Triathlon and began building the kind of team they actually wanted to be part of. In 2023, the Scheels introduced Branden Scheel Racing, which focuses on athlete relationships and connection. Despite being a team with athletes around the world, the Scheels strive to make their team feel like family and make each athlete feel seen.

“If we don’t personally know something about each of the team members, we’ve grown too substantial, which is why we sit between 100 to 150 members. We are committed to keeping this team on the smaller side,” Scheel says. The beating heart of the team is its Facebook group, where athletes connect through monthly games and seminars, get answers to their most pressing questions, and find encouragement.

Industry observers note that “On our team, every athlete stays until the last athlete completes their event because EVERYONE deserves to have someone cheering them on at the finish line. We’ve even had 15 people stay at the finish line for the midnight finish of Ironman Arizona for one of our athletes,” Scheel notes. “Having a tri family on and off course to cheer for you and celebrate one of the best days of your life is a huge part of our team culture.”.

Disruptors: Jaclyn Fahey, Tara Hofmayer, and Sami Saad.

Industry observers note that fifteen years ago, Jaclyn Fahey started a tri team through a bike store. As it evolved, Fahey recognized the need for a more affordable Long Island-based team, and Landshark Endurance was born.

“It began as a pizza-and-beer team with a triathlon problem, but Tara and Sami have helped take the lead. Because both are speech therapists and have the gift of gab, they’ve attracted a lot more members,” Fahey indicates. The open-level, co-ed multisport team supports members of all backgrounds with educational clinics and workshops, group workouts, and of course, social events that revolve around pizza and beer.

“By sharing our passion and experiences, we hope to show young athletes that success isn’t always measured by winning, but by perseverance, sportsmanship, and the courage to try,” Fahey says. “You don’t have to be the fastest or the strongest. You just have to show up for yourself, put in the effort, and enjoy the journey. At the end of the day, the greatest part isn’t always crossing the finish line – it’s the people who help you get there.”.

“I’m non-binary, and when I visit online triathlon groups and ask if there are any fellow non-binary athletes, it’s not uncommon that transphobes will flood the comments. I can only speak for myself, but the fear of discrimination, or being attacked verbally or worse, can be the most intimidating thing for non-binary and trans triathletes about tri clubs,” notes Ruth Carter, a lawyer and triathlete. “There’s so much misinformation out there about trans women and non-binary athletes, as well as assumptions that are not supported by research.”.

When Carter couldn’t find a triclub that promoted equal participation and respect, they created Mutants & Masochists, a tri club that believes in equal participation, recognition, and respect for all triathletes, and advocates for non-binary and trans triathletes.

“We’re just getting started, but I hope the club is a place where trans people can connect, both online and in real life,” Carter says.

In 2023, Hannah Bradbury was training to break an open-water swim record when she was rushed to the ER for an emergency surgery to remove her gallbladder.

Industry observers note that “My first thought when I woke up was, ‘When can I get back in the water?’ The answer was six weeks at least,” says Bradbury, who had already lost half of her thyroid to cancer in 2017. In an attempt to be part of sport in a way that cancer or a freak surgery couldn’t disrupt, Bradbury created Chicago’s North Avenue Swim and Triathlon Yo (NASTY) Instagram account to post about swimming until she could get back in the water. She also launched book clubs and threw happy hours to create space for people to be more than just athletes, from cancer survivors to diabetic athletes striving to stay in sport on their own terms.

Recent findings suggest that “Tri and swim clubs are great at training people. They’re not always great at holding onto people when they’re injured, sick, slow, starting over, or just burned out. I wanted to build a club that could hold everyone, from those winning the Chicago Triathlon to anyone rebuilding from injuries, or battling setbacks and the identity crises nobody warns you about when you’re sidelined,” says Bradbury, who faced another cancer scare in 2023. “While I waited on the biopsy, my friends kept me distracted by doing a 100-mile ride with me, covered in glitter, that we called the ride Centuslay.”.

Fortunately, the biopsy came back negative, and the women’s century became an official NASTY tradition every fall.

“Before NASTY I had a hard time making real friends with people who don’t just ask, ‘How was your swim?’ Through NASTY, I met friends who ask how they can show up for me,” Bradbury says. “NASTY has grown to over 340 members, and through this community, people have found jobs through a swim or a random happy hour, and even fallen in love. Sport has become an accessory to our friendships, not the glue.”.

“When I first got into triathlon in 2010, I was fortunate to have a warm, welcoming entry point into the sport. My goal with the T2 community is to pay it forward so others can also ease into the sport, learn to love it, and stay connected for the long haul,” indicates Bryan Mewes, who opened T2 Triathlon & Cycling, a triathlon-focused bike shop in Long Beach, California, in 2023. “The biggest hurdle for beginners is usually being overwhelmed by gear. That and the open-water swim. Once they realize that the shop is a space where they can comfortably ask questions and our group is built on encouragement rather than competition, that anxiety disappears fast.”.

Mewes explains that while it’s easy to say “everyone is welcome,” making sure someone is paired up with a partner at their pace or ensuring no one gets left behind takes actual effort that T2’s committed to making. Beyond the group rides, weekly runs, and bay swims, T2 brings people together off the course and keeps the vibe low-key and welcoming by hosting family dinners at local restaurants, beach days after races, and even a movie club.

“Some people only do our social events, while others only join our rides. What matters is that they participate in their way and see themselves as part of the community. That’s the core of T2. Training is just the anchor,” Mewes claims.

Disruptors: Ruth Marie Oliver and Team Rocket’s Race Directors and Officers.

According to recent reports, team Rocket Tri Club (TRTC) is on a mission to promote a fit and healthy lifestyle. Every month, the club organizes a themed, post-brick social, and throughout the year, it hosts various races, from a beginner-friendly pool swim to a duathlon and sprint triathlons.

Recent findings suggest that during the summer months, TRTC hosts Tuesday night bricks featuring a multitude of pace groups, ensuring no rider is left behind and everyone has buddies to ride with. And in the winter, the focus is on swim clinics and winter trail running.

“Our club president, Ruth Marie Oliver, has done amazing things, including growing our membership to over 300 people,” says Cynthia Mitchell, race director of TRTC’s Heel and Crank Duathlon.

To up the fun factor, TRTC has its own well-traveled bike box that members can borrow, adding their own sticker to its travel history and essentially bringing the whole team along for that athlete’s adventure. There’s also a TRTC hat that is currently “on tour.” It’s been spotted everywhere from Leeds, Alabama, to the head of Bob Babbit in Kona during the Ironman World Championship this year.

Disruptors: Corinne Geerdts Merten and Melissa Niemuth-Seamonson.

In 2019, Corinne Geerdts Merten and Melissa Niemuth-Seamonson relaunched TriBabes WI, a women’s-only, USAT-certified team, to provide a community for women of all abilities and ages to train together.

Sources indicate that “Some women join us purely to have the chance to work out with others for one, two, or all three sports. No matter what the sport or goal, we support each other without all the egos,” Merten states. TriBabesWI makes aspects of triathlon like climbing hills, changing tires, nutrition, and making a race blueprint less daunting through the clinics it offers. For TriBabe’s annual team triathlon, athletes can ride with a buddy for the bike portion.

It has been revealed that team offerings aren’t limited to the swim-bike-run. There are team hikes, skiing and snowshoeing in the winter, and opportunities to volunteer and shake a cowbell for others.

“We’ve donated our time and efforts to Breakthrough T1D, USAT triathlon events in Milwaukee, Ironman Wisconsin, and naturally Girls on the Run,” Merten notes.

Industry observers note that “When I was new to this sport, I went for a bike ride with a triathlon group and got dropped within moments,” states Topper, an author and coach who started WeREndurance in 2017. “If you’re just starting out, don’t look like everyone else, or just feel different from everyone, many clubs can feel elitist, especially when you get dropped. WeREndurance is nothing like that. It’s inclusive and diverse.”.

As the group’s triathletes grew older and more injury-prone, however, WeREndurance membership began to drop, so Topper proposed transitioning from a strictly triathlon group to a lifestyle group. Now, WeREndurance members who live locally in Long Beach, Upcoming York, can participate in monthly hikes and quarterly races, as well as pool parties, holiday parties, diner breakfasts, and even a psychic night. Members who live out of state can stay connected through monthly meditation sessions, a book club, and monthly/bi-monthly educational webinars.

Industry observers note that “These types of activities welcome everyone, including those who are injured or on the sidelines. This builds bonds and social connections,” Topper explains. “As you get older, you realize that sport is not only about being on the podium. It’s about community and having fun with your peers. The social aspect becomes just as notable as training and racing.”.

Disruptors: Brian Masayon, David Bahia, and Kristoffer Crisostomo.

In 2017, Masayon, Crisostomo, Bahia, and six of their friends formed a “silly” club to make training fun, and in doing so, others began taking notice.

“People started reaching out, asking how to join the team. I replied that there was no team. After the 20th inquiry or so, the nine of us decided to open 3P TRI to the public as a fun, drama-free group. That was in October 2017. By the end of the year, we had over 120 members join,” Masayon states. As word spread, the nonprofit tri club’s inclusive vibe attracted members from Canada, Australia, the Philippines, and Mexico.

While Ironman race entries cost athletes between $900 and $1,200, 3P TRI has removed the financial barrier entirely, offering clinics and free 140.6-mile races that are fully supported by the team.

“There is no timing chip, so members are not pressured to prove how fast or slow they are. Instead, they train and then enjoy race day with their teammates,” Masayon indicates. For 3P’s 140.6 triathlon, members come from different states to volunteer and help their teammates finish.

“People are intimidated by tri clubs because they have this impression of triathletes as being fast, quick, and strong. Our members, however, come in all shapes and sizes, and this becomes an inspiration to many people,” Masayon adds. “Nobody talks about speed and ability. We don’t play the comparison game.”.

Five years ago, a group of Upcoming Jersey moms tried a mud run. They had so much fun that one run turned into a road race, followed by group bike rides, and finally dipping their nail-less toes into triathlons, despite the level of intimidation.

Recent findings suggest that “At a 5K, you’ll see everyone from Boston qualifiers to families participating together, sometimes with little kids in tow. Triathlons can seem like a different world from road or obstacle races. They require training and preparation across three disciplines, and the level of athleticism on display can be intimidating. Sometimes it feels like there are no actual beginners, just really accomplished athletes with super fancy bikes,” indicates Merino, adding that if someone indicates up to ride with a mountain bike, they probably know it’s not the fastest option and don’t necessarily need unsolicited advice about upgrading. The same goes for swim form, running technique, or anything else. “If someone asks for pointers, we absolutely help them! Otherwise, the most encouraging thing we can do may be simply making them feel like they belong.”.

“That’s what Team Thunderclap is all about. We might not have the fanciest gear or be the fastest people, but we show up, give it everything we’ve got, and probably laugh a whole lot along the way,” Merino says. “At the end of the day, most of us aren’t competing for Olympic medals. We’re ordinary people doing extraordinary things in our spare time.”.

#194354. This Variation of Sun Salutation Is a Beginner-Friendly Energy Boost

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (693 w)

General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Yogajournal ↗ Open Full Page

This Variation of Sun Salutation Is a Beginner-Friendly Energy Boost

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (693 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Yogajournal

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In Yoga Journal’s Archives series, we share a curated collection of articles originally published in past issues beginning in 1975.
  • Practicing yoga for beginners is all about mastering the foundations of your flow.
  • This simple variation of Sun Salutation allows you to align breath and movement with ease—and minus any strain on your body—while boosting your circulation and energy levels.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In Yoga Journal’s Archives series, we share a curated collection of articles originally published in past issues beginning in 1975. This article about Sun Salutations for beginners first appeared in the September-October 1990 concern of Yoga Journal. Find more of our Archives here.

Practicing yoga for beginners is all about mastering the foundations of your flow. And at any level, a Sun Salutation is a welcome means of honoring the Earth’s many cycles—and getting your body and mind moving.

This simple variation of Sun Salutation allows you to align breath and movement with ease—and minus any strain on your body—while boosting your circulation and energy levels. It’s also a great option for those still working on their arm and abdominal strength, as well as anyone with lower back problems.

Move through this Sun Salutation as many times as you’d like, making modifications (like gently bending your knees) when necessary.

Feel your feet solidly grounded beneath you. Exhale and bend the knees slightly. As you inhale, press the feet down into the ground so the legs straighten. As you feel the downward force of the legs rebound up through the body, let the arms lift out to the sides and up over the head in response. With the palms facing each other and the hands shoulder-width apart, look up to the sky, greeting the sky gods and goddesses with an open heart.

According to recent reports, if you have a weak abdomen and lower back, be sure to keep your arms close to your body as you bend forward into Standing Forward Bend, to decrease the stress on your back muscles. As you exhale, bend your knees and bring the hands in Namaste (Prayer Position) down past your face and chest to the floor. Keep the knees bent and let the spine hang between the thighs. Use the exhalation like an anchor, feeling the weight of it drop down through the spine and out through the head. In more challenging variations of Sun Salutation, Standing Forward Bend will be one of the only resting positions in the cycle. Learn to let go completely and relax your head and neck to take full advantage of this moment.

Recent findings suggest that surrender yourself to the pull of gravity and to the Earth in Low Lunge. On an inhalation, step the right leg back behind you. (The leg with which you step back will be the leg that you later bring forward to complete the cycle. With each cycle, start with a different leg.) Allow the right knee to bend slightly and make sure that the left knee is directly over the left ankle. If this pose puts too much strain on your lower back or groin, rest your hands on two blocks placed on either side of your forward foot.

Recent findings suggest that as you exhale, bring the left leg back to meet the right. To make the position a little easier on the back of your legs, place the feet slightly wider than hip-width. Press the ground away with your hands and reach back through your sitting bones. Stay on the balls of your feet with the heels lifted to make the position easier on your lower back and hamstrings. Stay in this position as you take your next inhalation.

As you exhale, press the ground away from you with your feet, driving the spine forward until the shoulders are directly over the wrists, and the ears, shoulders, hips, knees, and ankles are in one line in Plank Pose. Lift the abdomen up into the shell of the pelvis so that both the front and back of the spinal column are equally supported. If you let the abdomen hang down from the lumbar spine, the hips will sink, causing the back muscles to overwork.

Hold this position as you take an inhalation.

Return to Downward-Facing Dog on an exhalation; Lunge on an inhalation; Standing Forward Bend on an exhalation; Mountain Pose. Bring your arms out to the side and over your head as you lift up on an inhalation. As you exhale, release the arms down by your sides.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recently, I asked you: where are you feeling most stuck with your fitness right now?

Industry observers note that hundreds of you wrote back. Thoughtful, honest answers. Thank you.

I’m working my way through all of them.

And one theme jumped out at me IMMEDIATELY.

One reader, let’s call her Supergirl, stated it this way:.

If you’ve ever had a great run (for a few days or a few years) and then couldn’t find your way back, this one’s for you, too.

I’ve heard this so many times in my coaching career. You were in a really good groove. Something knocked you off. And getting back on track feels incredibly difficult, and you don’t know why.

I’ve experienced this myself! I was in a groove with food logging. It felt easy. Then I took a break, and when I tried to start up again, I couldn’t get it going with any consistency for the life of me.

Here’s my take after nearly two decades of coaching: I doubt this is a motivation thing.

You were cruising at 70 miles an hour. You made a pit stop, and now you’re trying to jump the car straight back to 70. Instantly.

Of course that’s going to feel rough!

Another reader put it really well in their message to me:.

That’s driving with your eyes on the rearview mirror. And it makes anything smaller feel like it doesn’t count.

But smaller is how you get back up to speed.

Industry observers note that after multiple false starts with food logging, I realized I was falling into the same trap. And instead of forcing myself to weigh and measure anything, I gave myself a different on-ramp. Protein and veggies at each meal? Check. That allowed me to build back up again and find the groove that worked for me in this current phase of life.

Previous success can feel like a scorecard that you have to grade yourself against.

But what worked before might not work for you right now.

Recent findings suggest that and it’s key to remember that most of us needed an on-ramp the first time, too. That part didn’t change after some time off.

You know what you “should” be doing. Let’s put that aside for now.

Instead, let’s shrink down what our focus is. We don’t have to figure out the whole routine. Not the whole week. Let’s work on today.

Try this thought experiment with me: if you didn’t have any expectations of what this “should” look like, what is one thing that feels doable today?

It has been revealed that maybe it’s performing your warm-up routine. Or doing the first round of exercises in your workout.

Maybe it’s batch cooking some protein tonight, or running to the grocery store to stock up on some easy fruit and veggie options.

Try it out, and see how that feels. Is the resistance still there? If it isn’t, you’ve found the start of your on-ramp. 🙌.

It has been revealed that and if it still feels hard to start? That’s OK, too. We can choose a different entry point and try again.

In a recent development, if you’re in that camp of “I know what to do. I can’t get myself to start,” give yourself a different, smaller on-ramp.

Your on-ramp doesn’t have to be forever.

But it may be exactly what you need right now.

Hit reply and let me know what yours looks like.

Is Your Body Fat Percentage Holding Back Your Cycling Goals? The Answer Depends on Your Age and Ambition.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • For cyclists, body composition is a critical performance factor that goes beyond aesthetics.
  • Understanding age and typical body fat percentage ranges gives us valuable context for setting realistic and healthy body composition goals and determining whether our focus should be on fat loss, strength building, or overall health.
  • It has been revealed that 🚴🏻‍♀️ Ready to unlock a stronger, healthier you?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For cyclists, body composition is a critical performance factor that goes beyond aesthetics. It directly influences climbing speed, power endurance, and recovery capabilities. Average body-fat percentage averages and recommendations shift as we age depending on individual goals, and whether we’re a recreational rider or a competitive cyclist pursuing maximum power-to-weight ratio.

Understanding age and typical body fat percentage ranges gives us valuable context for setting realistic and healthy body composition goals and determining whether our focus should be on fat loss, strength building, or overall health. (It’s vital to note that body fat percentage and BMI (body mass index) are not the same thing.).

It has been revealed that 🚴🏻‍♀️ Ready to unlock a stronger, healthier you? Our Cycling for Weight Loss program will help you find confidence and consistency in your training.

There isn’t a universally “right” body-fat percentage. Ideal targets depend on sex, age, activity level, and specific goals, in addition to whether you’re prioritizing general health, recreational fitness, or competitive performance. However, there are commonly used target ranges per decade that coaches, trainers, and sports scientists use as healthy guidelines (which should be treated as approximate).

Let’s examine “average” body fat percentages guidelines by decade, what the average body fat percentages are for men and women in the United States, and the impact of different measurement methods (DEXA scan, home body fat scale, InBody scan) on results. These averages should be regarded as benchmarks for setting achievable, performance-oriented goals, not as rigid targets. They serve as a navigational tool rather than a mandatory destination.

20s: Competitive athletes: 6–10 percent, Fit/recreational athletes: 11–15 percent, Healthy range: 12–20 percent.

30s: Competitive athletes: 7–11 percent, Fit/recreational athletes: 12–16 percent, Healthy range: 14–22 percent.

40s: Competitive athletes: 8–12 percent, Fit/recreational athletes: 13–17 percent, Healthy range: 16–24 percent.

50s: Competitive athletes: 9–13 percent, Fit/recreational athletes: 14–18 percent, Healthy range: 18–26 percent.

60+: Competitive athletes: 10–14 percent, Fit/recreational athletes: 15–19 percent, Healthy range: 20–28 percent.

20s: Competitive athletes: 14–18 percent, Fit/recreational athletes: 19–23 percent, Healthy range: 20–30 percent.

30s: Competitive athletes: 15–19 percent, Fit/recreational athletes: 20–24 percent, Healthy range: 22–32 percent.

40s: Competitive athletes: 16–20 percent, Fit/recreational athletes: 21–25 percent, 50s: Competitive athletes: 17–21 percent, Fit/recreational athletes: 22–26 percent, Healthy range: 26–36 percent.

60+: Competitive athletes: 18–22 percent, Fit/recreational athletes: 23–27 percent, Healthy range: 28–38 percent.

Cyclists specializing in climbing typically aim for the lower end of these ranges, though excessively rapid fat loss can compromise strength and power.

While the ranges above are recommended guidelines, the actual averages for folks according to the CDC look pretty different. The following data on average body fat percentage of men and women in the U. S. has been collected through the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey.

Recent findings suggest that it’s crucial to note that the body fat percentage measurement method really matters. Home scales that measure body fat percentage can be quite inaccurate according to researchers. In my own experience, an InBody scan (which is the measurement method I recommend for a more reliable assessment, by the way) revealed that my body fat percentage is several percentage points higher than what the home body fat scale I have been testing had measured.

Industry observers note that however, even InBody results can fluctuate with hydration levels. DEXA scans offer the most stable results but are generally more expensive. The key is to track trends over time rather than focusing on single numbers.

In a recent development, when it comes to fat loss, aim for a safe and healthy pace of 0.5-1 percent of body weight per week, while prioritizing preserving lean mass through optimal protein intake and strength training. However, it can be tricky to determine how much of the body weight lost is fat, and factors like how lean someone already is, a person’s metabolism, and training intensity also play a role.

Industry observers note that as an example, in one study of female volunteers on reduced-calorie diets, participants were assigned exercise programs of varying intensity. According to the researchers, the women doing a moderate exercise program lost 6.2 percent body fat over three months on average, which added up to being about 2 percent a month. The intense exercise group lost an average of approximately 10 percent body fat over the same time period, which comes out to around 3.3 percent per month.

Understanding body composition is a valuable tool for cyclists looking to optimize their performance and achieve their goals. By considering your age, sex, activity level, and using reliable measurement methods, you can set realistic targets and tailor your training and nutrition strategies accordingly. Remember, it's all about finding the right balance for your body and your goals.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that rearview radars are one of our favorite cycling accessories because they alert riders when a vehicle is approaching from behind. Now Garmin and Waze are flipping that warning around: Their latest partnership alerts drivers when a cyclist using Garmin’s LiveTrack is nearby.

In a recent development, here’s how it works. Start an outdoor cycling activity with LiveTrack on a compatible Garmin Edge computer or smartwatch, and your location will appear in Waze as a moving cyclist icon. Drivers don’t need to be navigating a route to see cyclists; Waze told me the icons appear whenever the app is open, as riders enter the driver’s broader route area or immediate surroundings.

Waze indicates the alert comes when a cyclist gets closer, but it hasn’t specified the distance. In an email response to my questions, Garmin told me alerts go to “relevant drivers,” usually when the rider and driver are on the same road and traveling in the same direction. A cyclist farther ahead on the driver’s mapped route may also trigger one.

If several riders are together, Waze shows one icon to avoid repeat alerts. If they spread out, multiple icons appear. Garmin describes the grouping feature as “built-in clustering logic.”.

For Waze people, cyclist alerts are on by default but can be turned off in the app’s settings. Riders opt in to Waze sharing through Garmin, but only once. After that, sharing starts whenever they begin a cycling LiveTrack, whether they start it manually or set it to start automatically.

Sources indicate that garmin says any Edge computer or smartwatch with LiveTrack is compatible. LiveTrack requires a phone paired with Garmin Connect and cellular coverage; Garmin’s LTE-enabled devices can run LiveTrack without relying on the phone’s connection.

Recent findings suggest that no additional subscription or purchase is required. Waze states drivers see only a temporary alert that a cyclist is nearby, not the rider’s name, identity, or exact route. Sharing stops when the ride ends.

According to recent reports, this is not V2X, the connected-vehicle technology that has been simmering in the background. V2X systems let vehicles exchange information with one another, roadside infrastructure, and other road users, including cyclists. Garmin and Waze are taking an app-based route to a similar goal: LiveTrack sends a rider’s location to Waze, which can alert drivers using the app.

It’s a sensible idea, but it requires the latest apps and firmware, a Garmin rider who has opted in, a working connection, and a driver using Waze. It isn’t a substitute for cycling-friendly infrastructure, and it won’t fix distracted drivers or jerks in cars. But reminding drivers that cyclists are on the road is a step in the right direction.

Would you enable Waze sharing for your LiveTrack rides? If you use Waze while driving, would a cyclist icon or alert change how you approach the road? Tell us in the comments, or join me on Discord. I’d especially like to hear from riders who already use LiveTrack or Waze: What would you want to know before turning this on?

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, this short evening yoga routine is designed to help you release stress when you’re ready to wind down for the evening or let go of the day. It brings you a full-body stretch and a lot of relaxation. The poses are all either seated or lying down, so there’s very little effort required. You can even practice the yoga for better sleep routine in bed.

Industry observers note that the stretches are essentially yin yoga poses, except we’re staying in the shapes for less time than the usual 3 to 5 minutes that we expect from yin yoga. But these are all poses that you would find in a yin yoga class, so you could stay in any or all of the poses a little longer. The exact 15-minute sequence could be a 75-minute yin yoga class if you have the time or wake up in the middle of the night and are trying to go back to sleep.

Sources indicate that because you’re trying to calm the body and mind, these stretches are not about chasing sensation or pushing yourself into an extreme shape. Try to find a little more ease in each pose as you invite a slower, deeper rhythm to your breath, which signals your nervous system that it’s time to unwind and release. Every time you exhale, see if you can relax a different part of your body and let go of whatever is on your mind from your day.

In a recent development, these stretches are suitable for any experience level. No props are required. Let yourself linger and release into each shape and stay there for 5 to 10 breaths.

In a recent development, start sitting and then straighten your right leg in front of you. Option one, you can either do your Head to Knee Pose, which we call Half Butterfly in yin yoga, with your left foot to the inside of your thigh.

In a recent development, option two, you can stretch a little more through the hip and inner thigh if you take your left knee out to the side and your foot behind you with your heel tucked in toward your glutes. If you try option two and you experience any pain or sensitivity in the knee, come back to the first option.

In a recent development, then start to walk your hands in front of in a forward bend. Let it be a passive stretch, which means you want to let your back round and your head hang. Let gravity do the work for you. Stay here for about 5 breaths or so. While you are in the pose, can you let go of any tension in your arms, jaw, and neck?

Press your hands against the mat and slowly lift yourself back up to sitting.

If it’s not already, bend your left knee out to the side so it’s in line with your left hip. You want to create about a 90-degree bend in your leg and bring your ankle in line with your knee. Then align your right knee so it’s also at a 90-degree angle.

It has been revealed that press your left hip back toward the wall behind you and start to walk your hands back on a diagonal behind you. As soon as you start to feel that sensation through your left hip, pause and breathe into it a little. You can stay propped up on your palms, lower onto your forearms, or lie all the way flat on your back. I’m going to stay propped up on my hands. I find I get the best stretch this way. Breathe here.

Walk your hands in, slowly lifting yourself upright.

Recent findings suggest that bring your left leg straight in front of you. Cross your left foot over your right thigh, bringing your left foot to the mat outside your right leg. Wrap your right arm around your left and bring your left fingertips to the mat behind you and let them support you. Lift tall through the spine, pressing your shoulders down and away from your ears, then twist toward the left in a Seated Twist. Press into your left substantial toe and keep both sit bones on the mat. Breathe here.

Then take your Head to Knee or Half Butterfly on the other side, followed by Deer Pose or 90/90 and Seated Twist.

Lower all the way down onto your back. Pull your knees toward your chest. Then initiate a little pumping motion. So place your hands on the tops of your knees.

As you inhale, straighten your arms and push your thighs away.

Industry observers note that as you exhale, draw your thighs back toward you. Try to relax your legs fully so your arms are controlling the motion. As you do this simple motion, you’re trying to release your lower back muscles as much as possible. You almost want to feel like your legs are moving in water. Take a few more like this.

Recent findings suggest that the next time you bring your knees toward you, widen them toward your shoulders. Either hold here or come into Happy Baby by grabbing hold of your substantial toes with your two peace fingers, taking your elbows to the insides of your knees, and using your arms to push your legs open a little more. Think of pressing your lower back into the mat, keeping your head and shoulders down on the ground. Sometimes rocking a little side to side can feel really good.

Recent findings suggest that from Happy Baby, keep your right knee close to your chest and extend your left leg straight on the mat to stretch the hip flexors along the front of your left hip. You can take a few ankle rolls with your right foot by making circles, flexing and pointing through your toes, and making any motion through the ankles. Reverse the direction of those circles.

Come into your twist from here, crossing your right leg over your body to the left with the help of your left hand. Stretch your right arm straight out to the side. Think of relaxing your right shoulder down and trying to stack your right hip on top of your left hip.

Industry observers note that if you notice yourself obsessing over anything or going over and over a particular thought, just observe what’s happening. Notice that tendency in that pattern, and maybe instead focus on something else that’s a bit more tangible, like the physical sensations in your body from the poses or just the flow of your breath.

Come all the way back to center.

Industry observers note that straighten your right leg any amount, stretching the hamstrings. You can flex and point your foot a couple times.

Then come into Reclined Pigeon Pose by sliding your left foot in, crossing your right ankle over the top of your left knee in a figure-four shape, and reaching your arms along either side of your left leg as you pull your left thigh toward you. Only using a little arm strength. Try to relax your shoulders and keep your head on the  mat. Breathe here.

Keep your left knee drawn toward your chest as you release the pose and extend your right leg straight on the mat. Repeat your ankle rolls, Reclined Twist, and Reclined Pigeon on your left side.

Recent findings suggest that then you’ll set yourself up for Savasana, your final resting pose. Take up some space with your arms and your legs and then close your eyes. You might do a body scan, bringing your awareness to the crown of your head and slowly working your way down to your fingers and your toes, asking each muscle to relax, to let go, almost as if you could sink into the mat or mattress.

Allow yourself about two minutes here or more if you have the time. Just enjoy the silence and stillness. If you’re already in bed, maybe you stay here.

It has been revealed that start to deepen your breath. Maybe you move your fingers and toes a little. Nice and slow, roll to one side and come to take a seat. Find some length in your spine as you release your shoulders down.

Recent findings suggest that just pause here. Notice how you feel after just a few minutes of stretching and silence.

In a recent development, thank you so much, everyone, for doing this short bedtime practice. I hope you feel ready to ease into the rest of your night.

#194344. Reviewed: The EZ Hydro-Glide Swim Cap

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1064 w)

Reviewed: The EZ Hydro-Glide Swim Cap

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1064 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Triathlete

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Jumping into frigid water is nobody’s idea of fun – unless you enjoy the crippling pain of ice cream headaches without the pleasure of an actual ice cream cone.
  • In plain English: The Hydro-Glide is a potentially game-changing swim accessory that’s supposed to make you less susceptible to cold shock and heat stress.
  • Before we dive into the science, an key clarification: The critical technology here is not a cap, but a 3D-printed contraption that goes under your cap.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jumping into frigid water is nobody’s idea of fun – unless you enjoy the crippling pain of ice cream headaches without the pleasure of an actual ice cream cone. At the opposite end of the spectrum, swimming in very warm water can also crater your comfort and results. That’s why we were psyched to test the EZ Hydro-Glide Cap, a one-of-a-kind attempt to boost swimming performance and safety using wearable technology designed to enhance thermoregulation.

In plain English: The Hydro-Glide is a potentially game-changing swim accessory that’s supposed to make you less susceptible to cold shock and heat stress.

Before we dive into the science, an key clarification: The critical technology here is not a cap, but a 3D-printed contraption that goes under your cap. More on that below.

It has been revealed that but first, kudos to EZ Gains, a popular outside-the-box triathlon retailer, for attacking a problem that numerous triathletes experience – significant discomfort when swimming in very cold and very warm water. We’ve learned a lot in recent years about thermoregulation, and any improvements in this area could help many athletes, including friends of mine who’ve quit the sport after repeated unpleasant swims.

Recent findings suggest that EZ Gains’ approach is based on credible science. The company notes that your head plays an outsized role in your body’s response to ambient temperatures, given the extensive network of blood vessels and nerves just beneath your scalp. This rings true, as does the contention that regulating the temperature difference between the water and your head – both the initial gap and the ongoing variance – can mitigate the downsides of extreme heat and cold.

It has been revealed that we use insulated neoprene caps for chilly swims, after all. What if a single, more sophisticated solution helped us thrive in both polar and equatorial waters?

EZ Gains’ answer is a honeycombed high-tech foam and hard plastic wedge that sits at the top of your forehead under an (included) standard swim cap. Before putting it on, you can place one or two small thermal packs (also included) inside the hollow center of the wedge. These packs – and an additional thin heating strip – provide a cooling or warming effect as needed. In warm water, you can use a frozen pack or two to cool your forehead, which is meant to keep your core temp down and reduce heat fatigue.

You’re also supposed to use frozen packs when swimming in frigid water – say 60 degrees F or less – according to EZ Gains. The idea is to pre-condition your head to the chilly temps you’re about to encounter. This may sound counterintuitive, but EZ Gains states the pre-cooling technique can prevent cold shock, a serious autonomic response that elevates your heart rate and can cause panic and even cardiac arrest. The packs can also be heated for a touch of warmth when facing cool-but-not-arctic conditions.

For more preparation for swimming in cold water, read: How to Acclimate and Prepare for Cold-Water Triathlons.

According to recent reports, to evaluate the system, I tested it in various bodies of water over the course of five months, from midsummer to late autumn. My primary locations were indoor and outdoor pools in Boulder, Colorado, and our local reservoir. Water temperatures ranged from 84 degrees F all the way down to 50 degrees F. All of my swims were 45-90 minutes long, more than enough to mimic race conditions and assess how well the device limits heat and cold stress.

The TLDR from my testing: Some new technologies sound great on paper but don’t pan out in real life. Sadly, this device is one of those. On two of its three core value propositions, the Hydro-Glide fell short. I’ll tackle them one by one.

It has been revealed that first, EZ Gains says the cap will reduce heat fatigue and related complications – anxiety, increased heart rate, dehydration, and confusion – when using the frozen packs. I did notice a cooling sensation in the early parts of my summer swims, typically lasting 10-15 minutes. But while I appreciated the initial cooling, I didn’t discern a material difference in fatigue, judgment, or heart rate after an hour, even during my most intense workouts.

Recent findings suggest that second, the cap is supposed to prevent the instant discomfort and cold shock that many people experience when diving into frigid water. Perhaps I’m less sensitive than other athletes (my long-suffering wife might have an opinion on this), but using slightly thawed ice packs to pre-cool my head (as instructed) didn’t eliminate the ice cream headaches.

Industry observers note that in my experience, this kind of pain starts in my face and forehead, neither of which are protected by the device. It’s possible that the Hydro-Glide would help other swimmers, since physiological reactions vary widely, but I’d speculate that too much of your face, forehead, and neck remain exposed for the cold to be significantly neutralized.

Third, EZ Gains says the cap will protect your head when another swimmer clobbers you, which seems legit in the case of head-on impacts. A friend in my Masters group sustained a concussion last year when another swimmer swerved into her during a backstroke set. While I didn’t do any head-banging to test this claim, it’s reasonable to believe the Hydro-Glide’s foam would’ve absorbed that blow. Since the wedge doesn’t cover the sides or back of your head, though, it wouldn’t deflect all-too-common errant elbows or kicks to those areas during a race start.

There are two additional downsides to consider. If you have an XL melon like mine, you may experience discomfort from the pressure of the cone against your head. I did, typically after about 30 minutes. And if you’re even the slightest bit fashion-conscious, you will probably draw the line at looking like a Corythosaurus from Jurassic Park. The first time I showed up at the pool wearing the Hydro-Glide, several of my masters teammates burst out laughing. Someone compared me to a Conehead.

According to recent reports, which I could possibly live with if the results had been stellar. However, the Hydro-Glide didn’t deliver a meaningful upside for me versus a standard swim cap. While EZ Gains deserves praise for its waaay-out-of-the-box effort to improve swim safety and comfort, this product’s current execution doesn’t justify a $270 investment.

#194343. Latest Update: The Bivo Trio Mini Keeps Finding a Place on Our Bikes When the Temperatures Begin to Dip—Here’s Why

Latest Update: The Bivo Trio Mini Keeps Finding a Place on Our Bikes When the Temperatures Begin to Dip—Here’s Why

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1705 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • Your water bottles have probably frozen at least once if you ride outside in cold weather.
  • There are proven ways to keep your bottles from freezing—or carry hot beverages on rides.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Your water bottles have probably frozen at least once if you ride outside in cold weather. Usually, it’s only a thin layer of ice on top or a clogged nozzle, but that’s enough to be annoying. If you ride at low enough temperatures with standard plastic bottles filled with plain water, it will inevitably happen. However, it’s important to stay hydrated on winter rides.

There are proven ways to keep your bottles from freezing—or carry hot beverages on rides. Hot chocolate, coffee, tea, or Skratch Labs’ apple cider will warm your soul and lift your mood. And nothing hits better than a coffee stop in the middle of a cold winter ride, especially when conditions are dreary or sloppy.

Stainless insulated bottles broke into cycling about five years ago and have since exploded in popularity. They’re a proven way to keep water and hydration mix cool on the hottest summer days, and they can also keep hot drinks warm for many miles on winter rides.

The Bivo Trio Bottle, available in raw stainless steel and silicone-covered stainless steel versions, has become a bottle of choice on cold-weather rides. Read on to find out why, plus tips to prevent your bottles from freezing this winter.

FULL COLD WEATHER BOTTLE TEST RESULTS.

It has been revealed that cyclists have many different methods (often handed down from one generation of riders to the next) to help prevent frozen bottles. One simple solution is to start your ride with hot water. However, depending on the temperature and ride length, this can also freeze.

Industry observers note that using insulated plastic bottles, adding a high-sodium drink mix, and wearing a hydration pack or vest under a riding jacket are all tricks I’ve used (with varying degrees of success) to keep my bottles from freezing. And some riders still swear by adding a shot of booze to their bidon. However, while these methods may prevent icing, they still result in a cold beverage during your ride.

It’s hard to miss the growing popularity of stainless steel water bottles in cycling. Their use has boomed in the last few seasons as more riders have become concerned about microplastic contamination. Plus, these metal bidons, particularly the Bivo bottles, are in the cages of many cycling influencers.

Stainless bottles typically feature a vacuum-sealed double-wall design with a coated outer and a bare stainless inner layer. Since metal bottles are rigid, you cannot squeeze them like plastic bottles. (It takes some getting used to if you haven’t ridden them before.) And while stainless bottles are much heavier than plastic models, they are heavy-duty and almost indestructible—they dent and scratch but rarely break.

Recent findings suggest that bivo is the trend-setting stainless option and commonly available from retailers like REI, Backcountry, Amazon, or your local bike shop. The Insulated Mini we tested is 17 ounces and costs $44, or opt for the 21-ounce model for $5 more.

Sources indicate that I have ridden with insulated bottles at several points in my cycling life. But until last summer, I usually stuck with non-insulated plastic bottles for most of my rides, regardless of air temperature.

Generally, I prefer the feel of a regular bottle; 22-ounce Specialized Purist bottles are my go-to, and I occasionally carry a 10-ounce Purist Maker mug for a mid-ride coffee break. But I often skip stainless insulated bottles because they aren’t squeezable and weigh noticeably more than plastic bidons.

However, before a recent ride on a cold and blustery day, I filled an insulated bottle with hot chocolate and was pleased to have a warm treat throughout my 90-minute ride. So, like my insulated bottle test last summer, I applied a little science to see which insulated stainless bottles performed best in cold temps.

It has been revealed that for this test, I gathered several popular metal insulated bottles. First, I evaluated the bottles by measuring water temperature over three hours in subfreezing conditions. Then, I used them on rides in cold weather to determine which worked best from a functional perspective.

While the intent was somewhat scientific, I also strove to be practical—these are tests anyone can do at home. This testing was not performed in a controlled environment or with professional-level, calibrated equipment.

Since it was below 32 degrees outside, I was able to perform outdoor freeze testing. Like my summer insulated bottle tests, I filled the selected bottles with 400 grams of tap water (heated to 212 degrees for this test instead of chilled water used in summer). Then I placed the filled bottles on my front porch in subfreezing temperatures; I did this after sunset so sunlight would not warm the bottles. Every 30 minutes, I checked and recorded the water temperature of each bottle, in the same order each time, with a digital food thermometer.

Following the initial three-hour test period, the bottles remained overnight in sub-freezing temperatures for an additional nine hours. This tested whether the contents would stay warm for a full 12 hours (as per some bottle makers’ claims). Additionally, for reference, I subjected a Purist Maker tumbler (with 200 grams of water), an insulated plastic bottle, and a standard plastic bottle to the same tests.

The following day, I evaluated the bottles’ on-bike performance on a short loop in my neighborhood. I tested their use with standard and lobster-claw gloves (such as holding, opening caps, removing them from cages) and their nozzles’ function while drinking hot coffee (a medium-roast pour-over with some oat milk for my tests 😉).

Industry observers note that the results were clear: Insulated stainless bottles work very well in cold weather. They keep your beverage hot for an hour-long ride in 30-degree temps. For longer rides, your drink will experience some heat loss but will remain drinkably warm for three hours. The insulated metal bottles performed notably better than plastic bottles (insulated and non-insulated) for the full duration of the test.

After about three hours of exposure in the cold, the Bivo Insulated Trio Mini kept my coffee at a warm 119.8 degrees. This is only slightly below coffee expert James Hoffmann’s recommended coffee-drinking temp of 122 to 129 degrees. (Although I’m not sure Hoffmann would be pleased drinking three-hour-old brew.) In 12-hour testing, none of the metal bottles froze. Most bottles finished at room temperature after 12 hours outside in freezing temperatures.

On the bike, the Bivo valve works great, and the bottle texture isn’t overly slippery. The bottle shape is compatible with most cages, though it fits best in the Arundle Sport cage recommended by Bivo.

Nozzle Shield: Look for bottles with a cap that protects the nozzle. Typically, I’m not a fan of these shields when riding in warm weather—they flop around and get in the way when drinking. However, in the winter, caps keep road salt and slush off the bottle’s nozzle, and they also help prevent icing. Ones with a removable plastic or rubber shield are easier to clean; plus, you can use the bottles without the cap on warm days.

According to recent reports, vapor Pressure: Many of the tested bottles carry a warning about using liquids hotter than 180 degrees. This is to avoid scalding and burns from pressurized hot water when the cap or nozzle is opened. With insulated bottles, hot liquid heats the air inside the bottle enough to spray potentially near-boiling water into your mouth or onto your body.

Avoid this by letting your hot beverage cool slightly before pouring it into your bottle. For long rides (when using two bottles of hot drinks), save the hotter bottle for later in the day. This way, it has time to cool to a drinkable temperature.

Sources indicate that cage Compatibility: Since they do not deform or flex, metal bottles don’t pair with every bottle cage. Some stainless bottles have a loose fit in cages (bottles can even eject on rough roads), and some cage shapes do not allow some metal bottles to sit correctly, causing annoying rattling and buzzing while riding. Other cage-bottle pairings are so tight that it’s hard to remove the bottle while riding.

My advice: Check that your cages work before dropping up to $100 for newly introduced bottles that won’t fit. Some brands have specific cage recommendations on their sites. You can also read user reviews for the compatibility of different bottles and cages. Also, be sure to check the overall bottle height to be sure it fits in your frame.

Dropped Bottles: I do not recommend using metal bottles in mass-start situations; use plastic bidons for massive group rides or races. When a metal bottle is ejected from a cage on a bump, or you drop one (as is prone to happen with cold hands or when wearing bulky gloves), it ricochets off the road surface more than a plastic bottle. And while metal makes these bottles more durable, they do not burst open on impact or crush if hit by other riders.

According to recent reports, bivo shook up the bottle market when it launched its stainless steel bottles. The small Richmond, Vermont-based manufacturer launched insulated bottles shortly after, and cyclists have fallen in love with them. They work well, look good, and don’t have a funky taste.

In a recent development, as Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and New England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

#194342. What’s the Minimum Amount of Mileage You Can Do to Maintain Fitness? Experts Answer

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1362 w)

What’s the Minimum Amount of Mileage You Can Do to Maintain Fitness? Experts Answer

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1362 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that for some runners, taking a week or two off from running after a race is the hard part—they can’t wait to ramp back up their volume again.
  • Still, if you trained for months to build up the fitness, including your aerobic capacity, lactate threshold, and running economy, you probably want to try to maintain at least some of that afterward.
  • Maintenance mode also gives you the flexibility to be able to jump into a 10K or half-marathon on a whim, says Mike Sheehy, running coach for Team Abbott who has completed more than 100 marathons.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that for some runners, taking a week or two off from running after a race is the hard part—they can’t wait to ramp back up their volume again. But for others, crossing a finish line (of any distance) might feel like a natural point to take a break from the sport, or at least to significantly scale back.

Still, if you trained for months to build up the fitness, including your aerobic capacity, lactate threshold, and running economy, you probably want to try to maintain at least some of that afterward. That way, you can go into a spring training cycle with a solid base.

Maintenance mode also gives you the flexibility to be able to jump into a 10K or half-marathon on a whim, says Mike Sheehy, running coach for Team Abbott who has completed more than 100 marathons.

According to recent reports, keeping a steady mileage base also allows you to experiment. “This gives you a chance to try latest fuels, try new gear, a new pair of shorts, new pair of shoes, stuff you didn't like during your block,” Sheehy says. You could also experiment with pace. “This is a great block to think about moving your easy pace up 15 seconds to let your heart and body start adapting to that new norm.”.

In a recent development, if you want to strike a balance between giving yourself a well-deserved break and completely reversing all of your gains, the question becomes: What’s the minimum running you can do to maintain your fitness? And how long can I do that without falling back?

Here’s what running coaches and an exercise physiologist have to say, plus what other forms of exercise come into play in the maintenance phase.

GET YOUR MAINTENANCE AIMS HERE.

First, it’s crucial to note that taking a week or two off after a marathon and at least one week for the half is not only encouraged, it’s probably the best thing you can do for your body—and your mind.

Sources indicate that “The thing I encourage all my runners to remember is patience,” notes Sheehy. “Let your body heal and take that time.” He typically advises runners to take a full week off, then slowly add in easy miles without rushing to get back to quality workouts.

Then by the end of week two, you enter the true maintenance phase. “This is really an exciting time of running,” Sheehy says. “This is where we’re keeping 90 percent of the fitness with about 60 percent of the work.” He recommends taking the average mileage from your peak marathon training weeks rather than the single highest weekly mileage.

This tends to net out to between 20 and 30 miles a week in the maintenance phase for marathon runners and 10 to 15 miles a week for half-marathoners. That might look like three shorter, easier runs during the week and an 8- to 12-miler on the weekend. (Experts agree it’s best to run more frequently at lower volume for each run than do fewer, longer runs.) “That keeps you 90 percent fit, but allows you to enjoy running and not have the pressure of having to run six or five days a week and without having structured workouts,” Sheehy notes.

Industry observers note that andrew M. Jones, Ph.D., professor of applied physiology at the University of Exeter in the U.K., puts the minimum effective dose of maintenance running slightly lower—at 50 percent—though after about four to six weeks at half the volume, runners will likely start to see “more significant deterioration,” he says, specifically of race-specific endurance. (Running economy may be more resilient.).

That’s not necessarily a bad thing (and allows you to focus on other goals; more on this soon), and 50 percent is enough to preserve a foundation to allow you to pick up at the beginning of a 16-week marathon training strategy with relative ease.

Sources indicate that greg Laraia, a running coach at Motiv in New York City, agrees and provides this example: Say a runner finished Berlin on September 27 and intends to run London on April 24. After time off, he’d have them work back up to 50 percent of their mileage by October 25, then hover in the 50 to 60 percent of mileage range until early January when their London block would start in earnest.

Sources indicate that retaining intensity during the maintenance phase is arguably more important than frequency and duration, per Jones. “It’s impossible to give a minimum effective dose [for intensity] but ideally by week two [after a marathon] they’d get back to the pre-marathon training intensity but with lower volume,” he indicates, which might be lower duration and/or frequency of quality running. “Intensity is the key stimulus.”.

To hit this stimulus, Sheehy and Laraia both like to have runners add in strides (e.g., four to six 30- to 60-second strides as part of an easy run) before doing more intense speed workouts that could make their way back into the weekly schedule about a month after a race.

Sheehy provides an example of a speed workout he likes to include during the maintenance phase:.

It has been revealed that “The newly introduced race pace is something I know they can achieve that is apparent in previous race results and workouts; not some aspirational wish pace,” Sheehy indicates. “This will give them the confidence they need or maybe a wake up call, but it makes for a great starting point, and allows us to calibrate their easy paces and use the lower volumes to let their body (and heart) adjust to the new norm.”.

Sheehy cautions against swapping out runs that make up your maintenance mileage for other cardio, as it is key to maintain the specificity of running if you want to maintain running fitness. But he often adds in an indoor cycling day during his offseason on top of four or so days of running. If you dropped down your running frequency, an aerobic cross-training workout can support your fitness maintenance. Plus, it gives you a mental break, Jones notes.

Laraia says one case where swapping maintenance miles for other cardio could make sense would be when runners come off a fall race injured or worn down and simply need a break from running so much. “Running is always going to be the best option because running is the sport, but if an elliptical or a bike is going to make you miss [running] enough to want to do it again, let’s start there,” he says.

The maintenance phase is also a great time to focus on strength training, Jones indicates. Sheehy agrees, suggesting aiming for two to three days a week. You can do more volume (either via an extra day or more sets/reps) during this phase, but it’s still important to include one true rest day in your plan, Sheehy says.

According to recent reports, strength work helps to build neuromuscular capacity, improve power that can translate to speed, and strengthen your tendons and ligaments for the upcoming season, especially if you focus on heavier lifting. “Let’s get comfortable with the extra load and then let’s see if it makes running better and more efficient,” Laraia notes.

GET YOUR STRENGTH WORKOUTS HERE.

Laraia says signs that you may have pulled back too much include a higher-than-usual heart rate during runs or paces that feel harder than normal.

Still, it’s probably better to lose a little bit more running fitness in the offseason than to push yourself too hard, he notes. The former is going to put you in a better position to start a new training block in the spring, compared with the latter, which could lead to burnout and could set your next training cycle back.

“Realistically, you’re going to be better off taking the extra day versus trying to push through something if you’re early in a block or just trying to maintain fitness,” Laraia says. “I’d rather you be 100 percent recovered for every run versus in the build,” where it might make sense to go into a run feeling a little depleted.
