📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

In a recent development, just as the seasons change, so do riders’ preferences of which types of riding are preferred. For some, the season for taking the road bike on the local roads starts to fade as temperatures get colder and the gravel trail that parallels the road gets more appealing every degree cooler. It’s time to turn the road bike onto that gravel path.

Many of us have tried to take our road bikes on gravel, and there are steps you can take to get the most out of that underbiked gravel ride. After a recent lunch ride, the question was asked, “how much gravel can you take a road bike on?” Since gravel means different things to different people the easy answer is, it depends, but I wanted to stress test my road bike to find out.

I remember an old-school bike technician I used to work with told me, “you can ride any bike on anything if you are light on the bike and find the right line.” While that may be true, I wanted to find out how I could most comfortably take my road bike on everything that is off-road.

After taking my road bike where it was not designed to go, I learned some limitations as well as some simple part swaps to get the most versatility out of a road bike. Below I’ll touch on those limitations that I found and give you the most impactful changes you can make to your road bike before taking it on gravel. As Doc notes to Marty McFly in Back to the Future, “Where we’re going, we don’t need roads.”.

According to recent reports, the bike I decided to do the testing on is my Trek Madone, and I’ve had 700x28mm Pirelli P Zero Race tires pretty much since I’ve built up the bike. Those are by far my favorite road tires for all-around road riding—they’re fast, grip well through turns, and are surprisingly durable for performing so well.

Even though I love those Pirellis for road riding most of the year, I knew I would want to have extra rubber when I’m chattering along through some of the chunkier gravel I’d be testing on. I decided to swap out my tires for a set of the Continental Grand Prix 5000 in 700x32 mm. The maximum tire width on the Gen 8 Trek Madone is 32mm, but these Continental tires only measure just over 30mm because of the internal rim width on the stock Bontrager wheels. I could probably bump up the width a bit more, but I decided to keep the 32mm just in case I knock the wheels out of true during the stress testing.

Going wider with your tires adds an extra bit of compliance and more contact patch—both will help your ride quality when you take your road bike out on gravel. Part of the trick with going wider and bumping down your tire pressure is to make sure your tires are set up as tubeless. Setting your tires up tubeless allows you to run a lower tire pressure without the risk of pinch flats.

When you take your road bike on gravel, new bar tape can help by decreasing a little bit of the vibration. As you ride, most bar tapes compress a bit from the constant pressure of your hands. Some tapes may even start to unravel in sections where you keep your hands a lot—we used to see this a lot when customers couldn’t comfortably reach the hoods. There would be visible wear marks where the rider was keeping their hands on the bars. So replacing your tape at least once a season is a good idea to keep comfort up.

Sources indicate that out of all the bar tape that I’ve tried my favorite for taking a road bike on gravel is the Lizard Skin 3.2 mm Bar Tape. The slightly thicker tape reduces a bit of the chatter in your hands and it’s tacky enough that your hands stay stuck to the bars when you need them to be. This is true on wider tire gravel bikes as well, but it’s especially noticeable when you don’t have the same vibration dampening from a wider tire.

Sources indicate that flat tires happen on any bike, but they can be even more common rolling down a chunky gravel road on your road bike. Correct tire choice, tubeless setups, and riding a bit more cautiously than normal will all help prevent a ride-ending flat tire.

If you do get a flat just make sure you are prepared. At a minimum I typically carry at least one tube, tire levers, at least one type of inflation, and a good multitool. If I’m going to be far from my car, home, or if I’ll be out of cell phone service I’ll bring more than one tube—especially on an underbiking ride. I’ve been stuck out on a ride after burning through my lone spare tube, so now I like having two on rides like this. A few pieces of extra additions to your flat kit are: zip ties, a tire boot or dollar bill, and a tubeless plug kit if you’re running tubeless tires.

If you do get a flat just make sure you are prepared. At a minimum I typically carry at least one tube, tire levers, at least one type of inflation, and a good multi tool. If I’m going to be far from my car, home, or if I’ll be out of cell phone service I’ll bring more than one tube—especially on an underbiking ride. I’ve been stuck out on a ride after burning through my lone spare tube, so now I like having two on rides like this. A few pieces of extra additions to your flat kit are: zip ties, a tire boot or dollar bill, and a tubeless plug kit if you’re running tubeless tires.

Keep in mind it’s still possible to get flat tires with tubeless tires. A few years ago I took my road bike out on a local gravel ride and I bumped my tire pressure down to have a little more comfort and traction on my skinny road tires. I was rolling through some gravel and I hit a rock with my rear wheel hard enough for the tire to get pinched against the rim and put a good slice in my tire. Luckily I brought a tire boot (I used a dollar bill) and an extra tube so I was able to pedal back to the shop. In a pinch I’ve used things like candy wrappers or leaves as a very temporary tire boot. They don’t take up much room in your pack, so if you bring one in your pack there is no need to MacGyver anything on the side of the trail.

Recent findings suggest that if you only have a road bike and want to occasionally ride gravel I would strongly consider getting a second wheelset to ride gravel. If you have one wheel set for gravel and one for pavement you can easily swap wheel sets when you want to ride one discipline versus the other. Set up the wheels with a cassette with the same gear range, same size rotors, and the widest tires your frame and fork can fit—suddenly you have two bikes in one.

Sources indicate that as I was taking my road bike on exceedingly questionable terrain I thought, what would most people actually be okay with riding this bike on? As I rolled my Madone into some singletrack it was quickly apparent most people wouldn’t be stoked to follow behind me. Insufficient tire clearance, room for tread, and lack of suspension might be the first reasons you’d think of why a road bike isn’t going to perform well on singletrack (and you’re absolutely right). The geometry of the Madone didn’t give the handling needed to reasonably navigate through the tight trails in the woods.

The next category is where we start to delve into true gravel: doubletrack, jeep roads, and limited maintenance gravel. This is where I started to see the road bike actually perform reasonably well. The extra tire width combined with bumping down the tire pressure allowed the bike to feel reasonably compliant rolling through the varying surfaces. However, I really felt the times I caught a small rock that was hiding underneath the leaves.

In a recent development, riding local gravel roads and canal trails may have been bumpy, but it was most certainly doable. I noticed I was bumping around a lot, and I felt like I was putting in more effort to match my typical effort on the same segments I usually ride with a gravel bike. Especially when I started to ride through gravel after a bit of rain or sections that were covered in wet leaves I wished for a wider tire with more tread. I had to keep some of the descents a little more tame compared to normal, but on my local gravel climbs I was rolling up faster and more efficiently than normal. That is, until my rear tire would lose traction and I would burn all my matches trying to keep the bike both upright and going up.

Sources indicate that even with that being the case, so many modern road bikes now offer tire clearance to get a cyclocross tire set up. If I were committing to my road bike as a gravel-to-road crossover bike for the winter I would set it up with some fast-rolling tubeless cyclocross tires, put on new bar tape, put an extra tube in my flat pack, and let it ride.

Industry observers note that jason Griffin is Bicycling's Senior Health and Fitness Editor, bringing more than a decade of fitness experience and years in the cycling industry to every story. A former personal trainer and bike shop manager, he's lined up for crits, tackled enduros, but prefers getting lost on multi-day bikepacking adventures. Lately though, his toughest balancing act has been fitting trainer rides between family life and the next adventure.

#194316. Are Your Recovery Runs Too Long? Experts Explain the Line Between Productive Recovery and Added Fatigue

Are Your Recovery Runs Too Long? Experts Explain the Line Between Productive Recovery and Added Fatigue

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1345 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article.
  • Getting faster isn’t just about training harder.
  • While there’s plenty of advice about the importance of rest days and how slowly you should go during easy recovery runs, there’s considerably less discussion about exactly how long those runs should last.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Getting faster isn’t just about training harder. It also requires smarter recovery.

While there’s plenty of advice about the importance of rest days and how slowly you should go during easy recovery runs, there’s considerably less discussion about exactly how long those runs should last.

Industry observers note that massive picture, recovery runs should help you stay consistent between harder sessions; they shouldn’t leave you carrying extra fatigue into your next workout. However, simply running at an easy pace doesn’t guarantee an easy training load because the longer you run, the more energy you use and the more repetitive impact you take on.

In a recent development, so how long should your recovery runs last to maintain the volume-building, bloodflow-boosting benefits? And what signs mean it’s time to cut the run short?

We asked run coaches and exercise physiologists to explain how to find the right recovery run duration to ensure you’re not dragging for your next workout and when calling it a (rest) day might work best.

Recovery runs allow runners to increase their overall aerobic training volume without taking a complete rest day after every hard session, says run coach, author, and founder of 80/20 Endurance, Matt Fitzgerald. For instance, if the sole objective were to recover from quality runs as quickly as possible, total rest (a.k.a. not running at all) is more effective.

But receiving the benefits of recovery runs without elevating fatigue or injury risk depends on keeping duration within a certain range.

Industry observers note that “As a run extends, we’re also continuing to consume energy and introduce mechanical load,” explains Pamela Geisel, CSCS, RRCA-certified run coach, exercise physiologist, and director of Performance and Wellness Services at the Hospital for Special Surgery in Newly introduced York City. In other words, your muscles are still contracting, your body is still using fuel, and your bones, tendons, and joints are absorbing the repetitive impact of every stride.

If you extend a recovery run too long, the stress caused by this additional workload begins to outweigh the aerobic benefits of the run and can lead to the aforementioned heightened fatigue and injury risk, especially if you’re recovering from a particularly demanding training session.

This logic is exactly why experts all agree that recovery runs absolutely can go on for too long. The tricky part is finding the line.

“There’s no established duration or mileage at which an easy run becomes detrimental to recovery,” states Michael Landram, an exercise physiologist and assistant professor at the University of Scranton.

Instead, each person’s ideal duration depends on a variety of factors, including training history, current fatigue, nutrition, sleep, and the demands of any upcoming workouts, Landram explains.

Here’s a three-step checklist for making sure yours fall in the right range.

Usually, Geisel recommends keeping recovery runs between 20 and 40 minutes in length, but that window should shift depending on how much you’re accustomed to running.

In a recent development, for example, if you’re averaging around 20 miles per week, Geisel suggests aiming for approximately 15 to 25 minutes. If you’re regularly logging up to 60 miles per week, you can pencil in 25- to 45-minute recovery sessions.

And remember, these recommendations are starting points, not strict limits. Danny Mackey, head coach of the Brooks Beasts Track Club, notes he might prescribe a recovery run of just 20 minutes for an 800-meter specialist, while long-distance runners accustomed to running 75 to 80 miles per week can comfortably handle a 60-minute recovery run.

Additionally, it’s notable to take into consideration how long you’ve maintained your current weekly mileage.

It has been revealed that landram explains that a runner who’s consistently logged 50-mile weeks for several years may tolerate longer recovery runs than someone who’s only recently built up to that level. Even if both runners in this example have similar cardiovascular fitness, their muscles may not be equally adapted to the repetitive demands of 50-mile weeks.

So, if you’ve recently increased your weekly mileage, stick to shorter recovery runs and gradually extend their duration as your body adjusts.

If you’re relatively latest to running, are only running a few days per week, or have only easy runs on your schedule as you build endurance and consistency, you may not need a dedicated recovery run at all. Rest days allow for proper rejuvenation between workouts.

Fitzgerald recommends using your typical easy-run duration as a reference point and making recovery runs shorter and slower (zone 1, anyone?). If your scheduled easy runs are usually 60 minutes long, for instance, a recovery run—particularly one scheduled after hard, quality workouts—might last 40 minutes or less, at an even lower intensity.

If you’ve just completed a particularly demanding interval session, long run, or race, consider keeping your recovery run at the shorter end of your usual range. The same applies if you have another hard workout scheduled within the next 24 to 48 hours.

Heat, hills, and uneven terrain can also make an otherwise easy session more taxing, so it’s worth considering an even shorter duration in those circumstances.

Overall, your recovery-run duration should reflect what your body is accustomed to handling, rather than a mileage target you’re trying to reach.

Even if you’ve planned your recovery run carefully, it’s important to pay attention to how your body responds once you start moving.

Industry observers note that one of the first warning signs is a change in perceived exertion. If your usual recovery pace suddenly feels harder than it should or your legs feel unusually heavy, you may need to reconsider how long you’re running.

Geisel also recommends paying attention to changes in your stride, including heavier foot strikes and other form issues getting worse as the run progresses.

Sources indicate that the metrics available on your watch can also indicate a recovery run has gone too long. For example, an unusually elevated heart rate at your normal easy pace may signal you’re carrying too much fatigue, Landram explains. Though remember heat, dehydration, sleep, and stress can also affect heart rate, so pair it with how you feel to determine if you’re going too long.

If you’re feeling unusually tired during a recovery run, Shannon Hugard, a biomechanics researcher at the University of Oregon, recommends a simple midrun check-in. “If you’re feeling more fatigued or sore than usual, run that first mile,” she advises. “See how you’re feeling. If you’re still sore or fatigued, cut that easy run duration by about 25 to 50 percent.” If you’re experiencing pain that affects your stride, however, it’s better to stop immediately rather than push through.

It’s also worth paying attention to how you feel after your recovery run.

For Mackey, the biggest giveaway that an athlete isn’t recovering adequately is often what happens during their next hard workout. “If they’re struggling to hit their usual paces, feeling unusually fatigued, or showing a noticeable drop in motivation, I know it’s time to reassess their recovery sessions,” he claims.

If these warning signs persist, the best option might just be skipping your next recovery run altogether. A rest day, walk, or low-impact cross-training session can give your body a break from the repetitive loading of running, particularly when you’re dealing with lingering fatigue.

And if you think cutting a run short feels like a missed training opportunity, take a cue from the pros: “This is one of the biggest differences I see in elite runners,” says Fitzgerald. “They take pride in their restraint and ability to hold back, because they know it’s part of a more intentional strategy.”.

In my role as Mr. Money Mustache, I do my best to be your one-stop-shop for Lifestyle Guru ideas. So over the years we’ve covered not just the Money side of life, but also the even more vital stuff like health and fitness and the psychology of better, happier living.

In a recent development, but there’s one single area of life where all of these factors come together with an almost Nuclear Fusion level of synergy and effectiveness. And because of that, if I could have one single wish in the world, this is what I would wish for. It’s a change so massive that it would make every person on the planet better off and fix most of our problems in one grand sweep. And it’s probably not what you’d expect:.

That we immediately switch to building our cities and countries around people, instead of cars.

(and then fix all of our existing ones too, so that our entire world is built around person-friendly living.).

According to recent reports, the benefits of this are way bigger than almost anyone can imagine. We’re not just talking about eliminating a bit of pollution or a few traffic jams or car crashes. No. This is about far richer, healthier, and most importantly more fun living for everyone.

To put even conservative numbers to this, we’re talking about a life boost of over $20,000 per person per year, which compounds into well over two million dollars per adult lifetime.

On a nationwide scale, this would boost the wealth of the United States by about seven trillion dollars per year, which would compound into about 770 trillion over the next five decades.

Which happens to be more than the current total amount of human wealth on the entire planet.

Recent findings suggest that you will have a house that is both cheaper and more beautiful and spacious. Your body and brain will be healthier and stronger and sexier and cost a lot less time and healthcare dollars to maintain.

And all of our wallets and investment accounts, both public and private will be absolutely overflowing with surplus income, reduced expenses, and fuel an investment and prosperity boom like the world has never seen.

“Isn’t city planning just a stuffy thing that your city council does in the background while we’re all off living our lives?”.

Recent findings suggest that well, yes it is right now. And that’s the whole problem: cities are built by people whose primary job is to maintain the status quo and prevent disruptions. And those committes are elected and encouraged by crusty old companies and organizations, and plain old grumpy neighbors who just don’t have the vision to see what they are missing.

I’m convinced that if everyone could see through the smoggy haze of the status quo, we would all agree that this idea of a radical change is not only the best idea, but the only reasonable idea to even consider.

According to recent reports, so our job is to learn and explain just how major and how easy this is. And what it boils down to is pretty damned simple.

Whoa, that’s a bit of a surprise.

Recent findings suggest that so for the same amount of space you can have an entire pretty nice two bedroom apartment, or you can have just enough space for two (small) cars to park and pull out. But it gets even crazier than this. Check out this random intersection here in my own city:.

WHAT?! So every time you have two big car roads intersect, which happens hundreds of times in every big city, you are wasting enough space to build a luxurious, resort-like living area with about one hundred two-bedroom apartments and still have room for a pool, a dog park, a grocery store, a couple of restaurants, and so on.

This is just the beginning of the insanity, because I have only shown you two parking spaces and one intersection. The reality is that our entire cities are made almost entirely of stupid, expensive wasted space like this.

And the problem is so extreme that the only reason we think we need cars to get around, is because we have wasted most of our space on accommodating cars, which spread everything out so far (and made everything so loud and dangerous) that nobody feels like walking or biking!

Whenever you propose any great new idea, you’ll always get a bunch of smartasses who like to complain and resist change, without even bothering to think it through.

“But how are we going to keep driving our cars just as much as we do now?”.

Which is ridiculous – because the whole point is that as soon as you cut out all the huge wasted spaces we create to accommodate cars, you are suddenly FREE from needing cars so much!

Instead, you can just weave a brand upcoming city, with a bunch of variations of this beautiful resort which also include offices, grocery stores, climbing gyms and every other amenity.

And yes, you’d still have some roads between them, but they would be mostly for deliveries, emergency vehicles and people who need mobility assistance.

I hope you’re not going to make me ride the bus?

Recent findings suggest that I am all for public transit in theory, but to be honest I don’t usually have the patience for it. I don’t do lineups, and I don’t like to stand around waiting passively for my transportation to arrive – when it’s time to go somewhere, I just want to go, and go now, and get there fast. So my own personal choice is to take a bike for short distances (under 2 miles) or an e-bike for larger ones (up to about 15 miles).

Although this is often news to car drivers, bikes are much faster than cars for urban transport, plus they give me exercise and thrill, which is way better than being stuck at the red light with the cars.

If you take this already-superior method of urban transport and cut out the 90% of the land that we waste on accommodating the inferior cars, then you end up with a revolution: everybody gets where they are going ten times faster, at much lower cost, and has much more fun doing it.

And sure, there will also be light rail and faster buses. And sure, you can still hop in an Uber or even bring your own car into a city like this.But the point is that it will just happen much much less often.

Okay I’m convinced, but how can we actually accomplish this?

According to recent reports, mr. Money Mustache can talk a big game with all these fancy words and pictures, but the truth is that I’m way too impatient to put up with all the bureaucracy and complaints that arise when you try to actually change a city. I’ve been doing my best here in Longmont, and I have gotten just about nowhere. We’re still just stacking on more and more layers of ridiculous car shit where I live.

Thankfully, other people are much more patient and effective than I am at affecting change, and one group has made such incredible progress that you can now go LIVE in their first creation: a 1000-person car-free neighborhood called Culdesac Tempe. And as I write this, I am staying in a hotel right nearby, having spent the past two days touring and visiting and interviewing the founders*.

While we were at it, my Phoenix-area-house-fixing friend Tracy Royce and I also hosted a meetup for an enthusiastic group of our readers/viewers right there in Culdesac’s emerging central plaza.

Culdesac is Awesome and Could Change Everything.

If you only look at the financial spreadsheet, you would think this first Culdesac project is just going to be a highly profitable 1000-person cluster of apartment buildings, spread out across 17 acres of land. And while financial sustainability is indeed a key reason why this model will succeed, the money is the least exciting part.

When you look at these pictures compared to a normal housing complex, the main thing you will notice is that all the space that would normally be wasted on parking lots, is instead used for beautiful walking and gathering areas.

The next major upgrade is that they mixed in the amenities for daily life right into the neighborhood, rather than forcing all the future residents to get into their cars to drive out to find them:.

I was also impressed with just the feel of walking the Mediterranean-vibed spaces between the buildings, even at this early stage when everything is still under construction.

Due to the hot desert climate of the region, everything is built around providing shade, breeze, and reflecting heat during the summer, while also maximizing the joyful fact that there is no winter there (the coldest month of the year still has an average daily high of 65F/18C, which means palm trees, leafy gardens and fruits and flowers forever.).

With a setup like this, and 999 fresh neighbors to meet, I would rarely feel the need to leave the place. Which really cuts down on my desire to use a car. But on top of that, Culdesac has strategically placed itself in Tempe, a city right in the center of the Phoenix metro area, within walking distance of the main university and right on a light rail stop which allows you to reach almost everything (including the airport) for FREE, since an annual pass to the transit system is included with your rent.

But of course, you can also get around on foot, bike, e-bike, scooter, or hop into one of Culdesac’s fleet of rideshare electric cars for a trip to the mountains or whatever else you might want to do that’s outside of bike and transit range.

In a recent development, it’s insane. In fact it’s so good that I am going to attempt to move there myself at the end of 2023, enjoying my first escape from Colorado winter and celebrating the fact that my boy will be a legal adult at that time.

But even this is just a pilot project because Culdesac has much bigger plans.

From my conversations with the founders, I think they want to do this:.

So How Can We Benefit From This, and Support it?

And Then What Will Be Our Payback?

This whole change is exciting, and it is immense.

Understanding these ideas around city planning is the economic and social equivalent to being a doctor, and finding a 35-year-old patient in a hospital who is suffering from every chronic disease, but then discovering that they have been following a diet of Coke and Donuts for their whole lives and never been out on a walk, once.

In other words, the changes are so obvious, and the amount of win/win synergy so great, that every step we take towards making our cities better, and every car trip we eliminate, will absolutely explode our personal and national wealth upwards for generations to come.

The stakes just couldn’t be higher.

In a recent development, another collaborator in the overall effort for car free cities is a bank-founding multi entrepreneur local friend named Kevin Dahlstrom. His recent Twitter rant on building car-free cities from the scratch gathered a shocking amount of very positive feedback and interesting comments.

#194314. Breaking: 6 Myths About Max Heart Rate Cyclists Need to Stop Believing

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1494 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Bicycling ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: 6 Myths About Max Heart Rate Cyclists Need to Stop Believing

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1494 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that to dial in your training, it’s vital to know how to calculate your max heart rate because understanding this metric will help you stay within to right intensity on your rides.
  • Sources indicate that the formula, which is 220 minus your age, was developed by Dr.
  • Sources indicate that over the years, researchers have found other, slightly more accurate max heart rate calculations, like the Tanaka equation: 208 minus (0.7 x age).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that to dial in your training, it’s vital to know how to calculate your max heart rate because understanding this metric will help you stay within to right intensity on your rides. The catch? The most common formula for calculating max heart rate is not very accurate.

Sources indicate that the formula, which is 220 minus your age, was developed by Dr. William Haskell and Dr. Samuel Fox in 1970, and it wasn’t necessarily validated by research and involved data from a wide mix of people, including those with heart disease and smokers. As a result, the formula tends to overestimate max heart rate for younger people and underestimate it for older adults.

Sources indicate that over the years, researchers have found other, slightly more accurate max heart rate calculations, like the Tanaka equation: 208 minus (0.7 x age). However, it’s still a rudimentary system—like, “might as well use an abacus as a bike computer” rudimentary, states Cherie Miner, M.D., a sports medicine specialist in Birmingham, Alabama. “It’s been the standard for years, but there are a lot of variables that can throw off your max heart rate.” Some of those variables: how fit you are, how hot it is, and how much stress you’re under.

It has been revealed that because of these variables, there are also a lot of myths surrounding max heart rate. Here, we debunk some of the most common ones so you can get to know your heart, and use your metrics to train efficiently.

You’ve got to admit: This is equally horrifying and comical. But you can rest easy because it won’t actually happen.

“Most people have one to two minutes at their max heart rate—highly-trained athletes may have more,” Miner says. Expect to see your performance suffer very promptly if you try and maintain your max heart rate for more than just a short burst. Fortunately, years of evolving to survive prevents us from actually killing ourselves.

Industry observers note that the old-school formulas assume that it is the same, but Golich claims it’s much more nuanced than that. Max heart rate is largely untrainable and determined by genetics—some of us have hearts tuned like humming birds’ while others have the slow-and-steady type.

Recent findings suggest that although not perfectly accurate, age-based formulas give athletes an easy and accessible way to find a rough baseline of their max without undergoing rigorous (or sometimes dangerous, in the case of a sedentary person) testing. That said, The American College of Sports Medicine suggests age-based formulas with a lower standard deviation, for example, the Gelish equation: 207 minus (0.7 x age) or Tanaka: 208 minus (0.7 x age).

It has been revealed that no matter which way you calculate it, your max heart rate is not an indication of performance, Golich says. “If your max is 200, and someone else’s is 190, it doesn’t mean one of you is the better athlete.” In fact, Golich has worked with numerous talented athletes at both ends of the spectrum.

It’s good to remember that everyone’s max heart rate does drop as they age—but again, that doesn’t mean you’re losing fitness. Regular training and good nutrition will affect performance more than the fact that your max heart rate is now slightly lower than it was three years ago.

It has been revealed that in reality, it’s not your max heart rate that determines your fitness level. Being able to hold your max heart rate for longer and longer sessions is what’s key.

According to recent reports, heart rate is a reaction to work being done, not a measurement of actual work. For example, Golich says that if you ratchet yourself up to 200 watts (wattage measures your cycling power) for three minutes, for the first minute, your heart may tick along at 170 beats per minute (bpm). By minute two it may be at 180 bpm, and by minute three you could be pushing 189. But you’re doing the same amount of work the whole time: 200 watts.

Industry observers note that if you were to ride for three minutes with the intention of maintaining the same heart rate, things would look different. Say you ramped up to 180 bpm to start—you might ride at 200 watts for the first minute, but you’d likely have to drop your watts to sustain that heart rate for minutes two and three.

Golich indicates he prefers to have his clients train with power meters or using rate of perceived exertion (RPE)—a personal appraisal of how hard you feel you’re working—rather than heart rate.

“There are a lot of grey areas with heart rate,” he says, adding that being overheated, under-fueled, or even just hopped up on caffeine will throw your heart rate numbers off for the day.

It has been revealed that furthermore, the number displayed by your heart rate monitor or the screen on a gym treadmill may not be accurate. Sure, using a computer is certainly more accurate than the 220-minus-age formula, but Golich adds that because these devices take measurements every few seconds, they’re probably not dead-on.

If you really want to know your true max heart rate, an EKG is one way to go or a cardiopulmonary exercise test for even more accurate measurements, both of which require a visit to your doc or a lab.

Industry observers note that also, if you think that unless you’re hitting your max heart rate on every ride, you’re not working hard enough, here’s your license to chill. Max heart rate workouts should be done sparingly, Miner claims, since the ultra-high intensity can lead to injuries, extreme fatigue, and other symptoms of overtraining.

Plus, there’s merit to working in many different heart rate zones—from increasing your base fitness with low-intensity sessions to pushing the boundaries at your lactate threshold, and even tipping into some anaerobic work. If you only have two speeds—hard and harder—you’re doing yourself a disservice.

Heart attacks, while rare, happen to athletes at all different workloads. Even so, cardiologist James Beckerman, M.D., notes you’re slightly more at risk when working at very high intensities.

Sources indicate that “This is likely related to a combination of high heart rate, higher blood pressure with exercise (which is normal), and higher levels of catecholamines (hormones produced by the adrenal glands),” he states. “For people without heart disease, exercising at higher intensity is generally safe.”.

If you’re someone with heart disease or who has exhibited risk factors, however, it’s a good idea to talk to your doctor about safe heart rate ranges for exercise and even get a stress test, he indicates.

You’re not mistaken—your max heart rate for cycling really may be different than your max for another sport. Again, this is indicative of how variable heart rate is, Golich says.

Recent findings suggest that activities that are load bearing—like running—will generally push your heart rate higher, because you have to do more work to overcome gravity. Cycling, because it has the mechanical assistance of the bike, will generally produce a lower max heart rate. And swimming, which happens in a pool with zero-impact, may be lower still—since the water is keeping you cool, Golich indicates, heat will be less of a factor in raising your heart rate.

What exactly is heart rate reserve? According to Miner, heart rate reserve is the difference between maximum heart rate and resting heart rate.

In a recent development, your heart rate reserve can actually be a good measurement of how fit you are overall. “A higher heart rate reserve indicates better physical fitness,” she notes. That’s because, unlike maximum heart rate, a lower resting heart rate is associated with better fitness. “If your resting heart rate is lower, then your heart rate reserve will be higher,” Miner says.

According to recent reports, tamanna K. Singh, M.D., is a board-certified adult clinical and sports cardiologist and RRCA-certified run coach. She earned her medical degree from Boston University School of Medicine and completed her Internal Medicine Residency at Boston Medical Center. She completed her Cardiovascular Medicine fellowship at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, Upcoming York, New York and her specialty training in Sports Cardiology at Massachusetts General Hospital. Breaking: Research Shows This Is the Best Way to Balance Strength Training and Running

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1252 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There’s a reason why run coaches and personal trainers emphasize strength training in addition to running: Practicing both forms of exercise will allow you to build stronger muscles and increase your aerobic capacity at the same time.
  • But sometimes, especially after a heavy leg day workout, your body can feel pretty tired and sore and seemingly not ready to take on miles.
  • In a recent development, so if you’ve ever been tempted to skip the weights today in favor of a better run tomorrow, consider the advantages of strength training.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There’s a reason why run coaches and personal trainers emphasize strength training in addition to running: Practicing both forms of exercise will allow you to build stronger muscles and increase your aerobic capacity at the same time. Combining strength training and a running schedule means you boost your fitness in multiple ways.

But sometimes, especially after a heavy leg day workout, your body can feel pretty tired and sore and seemingly not ready to take on miles. This isn’t just in your head. According to a review of 132 studies, it takes a full day or two more to recover from resistance training than it does a high-intensity run.

In a recent development, so if you’ve ever been tempted to skip the weights today in favor of a better run tomorrow, consider the advantages of strength training. Not only does it just feel good to move your muscles through full ranges of motion, especially after sitting all day, but it can also pay off in the long run for your run performance and overall health. In fact, several studies point to better running economy, as well as VO2 max and anaerobic threshold, when following a program that incorporates both endurance training and strength training.

Recent findings suggest that instead of ditching strength exercises to focus on mileage, the key is creating a strength training schedule that optimally fits into your run training. After all, strength training is supposed to help, not harm, your running. Here’s how to achieve that.

According to recent reports, get the strength initiative that works for all runners! Race-Ready Strength, our new progressive 4-week training program, will get you in the best shape to reach your racing goals.

It has been revealed that to get it right, you need to understand how your body reacts to moving heavy stuff. Picture pushing a hand truck 50 feet. Pretty easy. That’s running—your body is the hand truck and it moves its own weight rather effortlessly. Now slide the hand truck under a fridge and push it just five feet. A lot more difficult. That’s mechanical loading; it’s why 10 heavy squats feels so much more challenging than 1,000 foot strikes.

The reason strength training makes you faster is because it lowers the amount of energy required to hit a certain pace, explains Kenji Doma, Ph.D., a sports and exercise scientist at James Cook University in Queensland, Australia, and author of a 2014 study on strength training and running performance published in the European Journal of Sports Science.

In a recent development, doma has also studied the effects of combining aerobic exercise and strength training on muscle hypertrophy and strength, as published in a Sports Medicine systematic review and meta-analysis in 2022. The researchers found that combining the two types of training doesn’t hinder strength and muscle-building gains, but can compromise explosive strength gains when performed in the same session—something to consider if that’s your goal.

Industry observers note that what’s important to note is that when you lift weights, your brain alters its neural recruitment pattern, calling up the most fatigue-resistant muscle fibers so you exert less energy. That’s why you don’t want to skimp on strength training. Doma’s research offers guidance on how best to combine mile repeats and repetitions in the gym for a more well-rounded running and strength training schedule.

In the study that focused specifically on running performance, 15 runners of a wide range of ability and average weekly mileage did different strength-training sessions on three occasions. One workout was a high-intensity, total-body session, one was high intensity but for legs only, and one was a low-intensity, total-body workout.

Industry observers note that six hours after each workout, the runners did a treadmill test for 10 minutes at 70 percent of ventilatory threshold pace (easy), then 10 minutes at 90 percent of threshold pace (roughly close to half marathon pace), and then as long as possible at 110 percent of threshold pace. The runners also did the treadmill test at the outset of the study, to get a benchmark for how they would perform when fresh.

In a recent development, the high-intensity strength workouts significantly lessened the runners’ time to exhaustion at the end of the treadmill test. In the benchmark test, they’d lasted an average of close to five minutes at 110 percent of threshold pace. After each of the high-intensity strength sessions, time to exhaustion was almost a minute less, suggesting that the hard weight workouts six hours earlier had dramatically decreased the runners’ ability to sustain fast running.

Doma states his findings have practical implications for how runners should arrange their workouts.

First, he advises not to schedule a hard running workout later in the day of a weight session. “Running at maximal effort is impaired six hours [after] lower-extremity resistance training, and therefore trained to moderately-trained runners will need more than that to recover for running sessions set at high intensities,” he says.

It has been revealed that plus, running at maximal effort is still impaired 24 hours after lower-extremity resistance training, according to Doma. “Therefore, in the case of trained and moderately-trained runners undertaking high-intensity running sessions after lower-extremity resistance training, they may need more than one day to recover.”.

In a recent development, doma also found that running performance at lower intensities was unaffected by the weight workouts. “Runners could undertake strength training and running sessions on the same day six hours apart as long as the running session is set at submaximal intensities,” Doma says. In other words, if you have an easy, long run, or recovery run on the schedule, it’ll be fine to double up that day, as long as workouts are more than six hours apart.

Sources indicate that if possible, Doma suggests arranging your schedule so that on days that you run and lift, running comes first. “I found that lower-extremity resistance training performed six hours prior to running sessions at moderate to high intensities cause carryover effects of fatigue the next day to a greater extent than the reverse sequence,” he notes. “Therefore, if undertaking lower-extremity resistance training and running sessions on the same day, it is best to undertake a running session before a strength training session. For example, running in the morning before work and lower-extremity resistance training in the evening after work.”.

In this scenario, it would make sense to have that morning run be one of your harder workouts of the week. Your workout the following day would then be an easy recovery run, which would be warranted even without the evening lifting, but is that much more called for on the basis of Doma’s research.

This sequence would also mesh with many coaches’ recommendation to have great discrepancy between your hard and easy days, so that you can better recover from your toughest workouts—instead of including hard elements of non-running training on your easy running days.

Sources indicate that scott is a veteran running, fitness, and health journalist who has held senior editorial positions at Runner’s World and Running Times. Much of his writing translates sport science research and elite best practices into practical guidance for everyday athletes. He is the author or coauthor of several running books, including Running Is My Therapy, Advanced Marathoning, and Meb for Mortals. Scott has also written about running for Slate, The Atlantic, the Washington Post, and other members of the sedentary media. His lifetime running odometer is past 110,000 miles, but he’s as much in love as ever.

Runners are a varied breed. Some crave the routine of a daily run and the endorphin boost it brings. Sources indicate that you can depend on your daily run—it’s what gives you energy and lifts your mood, no matter what else the day may bring. The Nike Pegasus line has offered that same dependability for more than four decades, and the technology just keeps getting better.

The reason why the Pegasus Plus 2 works for daily, all-purpose running is its technology: Superlight ZoomX foam in the heel pairs with an exposed Air Zoom unit in the forefoot to deliver comfort and energy return that powers up every mile. Up top, a sleek mesh material offers both support and flexibility without letting your foot overheat, while a revamped forefoot shape gives your toes a little more wiggle room. The Pegasus Plus 2 is also a good option to slip on for easy and slower recovery runs. Responsive and comfy without being super stacked, this shoe is the ultimate workhorse in your running closet.

For long runs and marathon training, you want max cushioning, like what’s found in Nike’s Vomero 18. Lightweight ZoomX foam stacked on top of responsive ReactX foam in the shoe’s midsole results in a plushy landing that has you feeling like you’re landing on a cloud with every step. Considering that the Vomero 18 is 13 percent more responsive than previous React technology (per the company’s own measurement), your legs feel less fatigued even as the miles add up.

Sources indicate that an increased rocker design and pods placed strategically around the outsole allow for better push-off and smoother heel-to-toe transitions. The breathable engineered mesh material up top and plush padding in the tongue and lining help your feet stay cool and comfortable. This super cushy shoe that runs effortlessly is one of the reasons why RW shoe testers gush about it.

For those who like to customize their kicks, the shoe is part of the “Nike by You” line, allowing you to pick features like color and accents and even add your own text in the heel, tongue, and forefoot.

You’re not just a runner. You also rule the weight room, enjoy a good cardio class, and have been known to dabble in metabolic conditioning workouts. If you’re looking for an all-purpose training shoe, Nike’s versatile Free Metcon 7 fits whatever your workout ask. This sleekly designed cross-training shoe lets you have it all, from supporting multi-direction movements on the gym floor to dynamic cushioning when you want to hit the treadmill.

The shoe finds its multiuse purpose with a flexible design that features softer foam in the midsole and firmer foam in the heel for added stability. Plus, the full-length rubber outsole helps with traction on a variety of surfaces, including turf, concrete, and gym floors. You’ll also appreciate the webbed lacing and midfoot containment system designed to keep your foot firmly in place as you move around.

For those who want a mixed-terrain shoe that can hit the road and trail and also handle inclement weather like rain and snow, the Vomero 18 Gore-Tex is a great choice. These waterproof shoes are designed to take on puddles, pebbles, rocks, and roots without missing a beat.

Recent findings suggest that the shoe has all the same stacked ZoomX and ReactX performance cushioning as the Vomero 18, plus a Gore-Tex waterproof liner to help your feet stay dry without getting too sweaty. The Storm-Tread outsole is specifically engineered for wet and slippery conditions, with an enhanced rubber compound for stronger grip and a thoughtful outsole pattern that keeps you grounded even on icy surfaces. In a recent development, if you are looking for a shoe to race in, the long-awaited Alphafly 4 is an upgrade to Nike’s popular carbon-plated shoe. That’s accomplished through its upgraded RF Air Zoom cushioning unit underfoot that uses vibration and frequency to create a smooth, comfortable ride, while the carbon fiber Flyplate gives you extra energy return to power through every mile. A slightly wider platform design compared to the Alphafly 3 also provides more stability so you can feel confident even on quick turns. And the wispy Atomknit 2.0 upper offers enough support to keep your foot firmly in place with as little added weight as possible.

In a recent development, your shakeout run after a marathon or ultra should be about comfort at an easy pace. Think plenty of cushioning, a smooth, bouncy ride, and an unfussy upper. The Nike Vomero Premium ticks all those boxes, making it a good choice to slip on for post-marathon recovery runs.

In a recent development, tired legs will appreciate a midsole that’s made up of ZoomX foam surrounding two energy-boosting Air Zoom units—one in the forefoot and one at the heel. The result is a light, comfortable ride with energy return that makes each step feel effortless and propels you easily along your route. You’ll want to wear this shoe for your daily runs for weeks after your 26.2-mile-and-beyond races.

According to recent reports, who doesn’t want to slip into something comfortable after a long run, or just a long day? The Nike ReactX Rejuven8 is just the thing, with a design that’s created to elicit all the aahs you can imagine. Thanks to React X technology in the upper and midsole, your feet will be surrounded in soft, responsive comfort. There’s extra room in the forefoot to allow your toes to rest and ventilation holes to allow your feet to breathe. Walking is easy and fluid because the sticky rubber outsole adds grip to the ground below you; therefore, no additional balancing act to get from one place to another. The result: A recovery shoe you’ll never want to take off.

According to recent reports, we all love getting gifts, but shopping for shoes can be tricky when you’re not the one who will be wearing them. A little advanced knowledge can make a big difference in ensuring your present is truly appreciated. Here are some buying tips:.

Recent findings suggest that check what they already run in. If you can, look at the label inside a pair of running shoes they like, or ask someone who knows. Note the model, size, and width—running-shoe sizing may differ from their dress-shoe size—as well as any preferences, such as cushioning or toe-box room.

Check the return policy. See if the store has any specific limits on returns and exchanges, and if you can get a gift receipt so your giftee has the option to exchange the shoe for a different size.

Keep fit in mind. Remember that footwear largely depends on individual fit, with some shoes running bigger or smaller than the given size. When possible, avoid final sales (where the shoe is not eligible for returns) just in case there’s a fit issue.

Industry observers note that the Nike running shoes best suited for long runs and marathon training are the Nike Vomero 18. You want to make sure your shoe offers both stability and support to reduce injury risk and protect your joints. Many distance runners today prefer shoes with maximalist midsoles, which feature a large stack of foam to cushion against impact, as well as energy return rocker designs for faster push-off and landings. These are all things the Nike Vomero 18 delivers on.

When it comes to race-day itself, especially for half-marathons and full-marathons, many runners seeking a time goal prefer performance shoes like Nike’s Alphafly 4, which have a thin carbon plate for strong energy return and maximum speed.

When looking for a recovery-run shoe, you want one that feels comfortable and provides plenty of support and a smooth, stable ride without being overly technical. The Nike Vomero Premium is the best Nike running shoe for easy recovery runs because it’s a shoe that delivers full-length cushioning and a roomy fit so your feet stay happy.

To choose the right size and width for Nike running shoes, go to a store that specializes in running shoes and try a few pairs on. Most running stores will let you jog around the floor (and some even let you jog around the block) so you have a sense of what works best. Running shoes should feel roomy but not so much that your feet move around a lot. You should be able to fit about a thumbnail’s width between your longest toe and the front of the shoe. There also shouldn’t be any pressure on your pinky toe, and only a little bit of pressure on your big toe.

If you’re experiencing side pinching, bulging or spilling over, or flat arches, a wide shoe may be for you. These Nike models are available in wide widths: Downshifter 14, Pegasus 42, Revolution 8, Structure 26, Vomero Plus and Vomero 18.

Recent findings suggest that I know, my hobby is not normal. Here’s what they noted.

According to recent reports, think triathlon is wild? Take on eight sports. You go from kayaking to mountain climbing to mountain biking, then trail running, a swim across a lake to get to your road bike, and after 50 miles of biking, you tie up your road running shoes for a foot-race to your final event: paddleboarding to the finish line.

Sources indicate that the only problem is, I can’t say it with a straight face. Triathlon (or a made-up octo-thlon) sounds about as crazy as cooking an eight-course meal with one oven for 15 people to gather around a table that really only seats six.

Once you do it a few times, muscle memory kicks in, and the logistics feel less overwhelming. So yes, I’m still doing that triathlon thing, and you can too.

– Rebekah Brately, associate editor.

In a recent development, everyone’s doing those Ironman races these days. I’m not sure when it became normal to casually jump into a full-distance race before the shorter ones, but here we are. Some people are even doing multiple, in a row.

I used to be one of the youngest on the start line. Now I’m surrounded by the next generation telling me their HRV scores, how many gels they’re trying to stomach because some pro is eating 200 grams of carbohydrates an hour, and why I NEED to start taking creatine. And don’t forget Bicarb, yes, that bicarb under your sink … don’t get me started.

Oh, and they’ve got an ultramarathon and a Hyrox lined up in the next three weeks, too.

According to recent reports, it seems my “crazy weird” endurance hobby has really caught on. You’d better jump on quick before you get left behind with me. Now pass me more yams because … Magnus, carbs, and whatnot.

– Travis Mundell, social media manager.

Recent findings suggest that so first you run, then you hop in the water. No, you don’t take off your shoes, that’s part of it. Then you swim. Really far? No, not at once, but in aggregate. (What does aggregate mean? Don’t worry about it, [nephew name redacted to prevent family squabbling].) Then you get out of the water. Oh, and you can use paddles and a swim buoy; it helps with the shoe problem. And you run again.

Did I mention you usually do it with a partner, so you’re tied together? Most of the running is off-road … Yes, you’re tied together; it’s for safety. I think. And you do it over and over for hours. My time? Honestly, I can’t even remember how long it took me; it was a long time. And there’s like a dozen transitions. Well, maybe “transitions” isn’t accurate; it’s not like in triathlon at all. And you end up swimming and running really far. How far? I can’t remember, and it changes, and it doesn’t really matter.

Oh, and there’s some really cool gear that you can use, like wetsuits that zip down to cool you off and have removable arm warmers and…wait, where did everyone go?

– Chris Foster, editor-in-chief.

You’ve shown such interest in triathlon every time I see you, Uncle Bill, so I signed you up to do a race with me next spring! Don’t worry, it’s a short one – only about 16 miles total. I’ll see you in the pool tomorrow morning for your first workout! [Walks away in search of pie.].

It improves on the Varia RTL515—our longtime benchmark, which is also on sale—with increased detection range, same-speed vehicle tracking, longer battery life, and a brighter taillight. Plus, when paired with a newer Garmin cycling computer, the RearVue 820 will track the lane location and size of approaching vehicles.

According to recent reports, still using your phone to track your rides? A cycling computer is a safer, more accurate way to navigate, display key riding metrics, and capture data from devices like heart rate monitors and power meters. Garmin’s Edge 540 packs computing power, battery life, and function into an 80-gram package. It’s a great upgrade for any road, mountain, gravel, or fitness rider.

Wahoo’s Elemnt Bolt 3 is a favorite of our editors and test riders for its small size, accuracy, and ease of use. The Bolt features a 2.3-inch full-color display, 20-hour battery life, and an 85-gram weight. For simple operation and a lower price, the Bolt uses buttons instead of a touchscreen.

Keep your hot drinks warm on cold winter rides. CamelBak’s Podium bottles are popular among gravel and off-road riders due to their open/closed twist-lock cap. The Podium Steel is a vacuum-sealed insulated stainless steel version of the brand’s classic plastic Podium model. It’s a classy-looking bottle and available in several colors. Plus, CamelBak offers custom printing on these bottles through its site.

Industry observers note that last winter, I tested 8 of the top insulated bottles in winter conditions. Read about the testing and results: “Some Insulated Bike Bottles Promise 12 Hours of Hot Drinks. Which Ones Survived Our Experts’ Sub‑Freezing Tests?”.

It has been revealed that cycling radars are a new technology that gets a lot of attention for keeping riders safe on the road. Mirrors have been around for generations and do a great job, never require charging, and don’t chirp endlessly in traffic. I added a Spurcycle mirror to my custom bike this summer. I love its simplicity and clean looks—it doesn’t look out of place, even on high-end race bikes.

In a recent development, “Flat pedals win medals” is an age-old bike saying. While many riders have switched to clipless pedals for road and gravel, many prefer flats for mountain biking and commuting. They’re intuitive, compatible with almost any shoes, and you never have to worry about unclipping too late. OneUp’s Composite Pedals are lightweight and durable—plus they’re available in two sizes and six colors.

According to recent reports, lazer’s Tonic Kineticore helmet performs much better than its $80 MSRP suggests—and at $60 (25% off), it’s a steal. At 240 grams, the Tonic is relatively light for its price. It features a modern road aesthetic and has comfortable, easy-to-adjust straps. Lazer offers the Tonic in four sizes, and four color options are on sale. It’s a solid pick for any road or gravel rider.

In a recent development, wahoo reinvented indoor training when it released its original Kickr in 2012. Now on its sixth generation, the Kickr remains our top pick for high-performance indoor smart trainers. The Kickr is super accurate, folds easily for storage, and is stable during workouts. The latest version adds WiFi connectivity, which enhances connection speeds during Zwift rides and races.

In a recent development, garmin’s Tacx Neo 2 sits at the top of the performance-trainer pyramid. However, most indoor cyclists don’t need its pricey features. The Tacx Flux 2 has a large 7.6 kg flywheel with up to 2,000 watts of resistance (more than enough for almost any rider). It also simulates gradients up to 16%, to replicate the toughest climbs in virtual cycling worlds such as Zwift and Rouvy.

Tights are a must-have for riding in temps below 45 degrees. Pearl Izumi’s Quest tights feature a soft ThermaFleece lining, thigh pockets to hold your phone or snacks, and a single-density chamois pad. Men’s and women’s sizing is available.

WOMEN’S QUEST TIGHTS - $110 $82.

Stay warm on winter rides and commutes with Pearl Izumi’s AmFib gloves. These gloves feature Primaloft insulation, AmFib material to block wind and rain, and synthetic leather palms for grip. Unlike many winter gloves, they’re touchscreen compatible. The AmFibs also have an extended cuff, so cold air doesn’t get into your gloves or jacket.

It has been revealed that rapha makes excellent, high-performance cycling apparel. However, it tends to be too pricey for many riders. The Core line is Rapha’s base-level kit, but it has much of the fit and comfort of the brand’s premium clothing. These bibs use the same chamois found in the more expensive Classic bibs. With proper care and washing, the bibs will last you several seasons.

Recent findings suggest that we love these shorts because they’re great for hot summer rides and sweaty indoor workouts in the dead of winter. Plus, they have thigh pockets to hold your cell phone or snacks while you ride.

If you log a lot of time on the trainer, it’s worth refreshing your shorts regularly; worn-out shorts are a recipe for discomfort. The extra sweat from indoor rides breaks down the chamois faster than outdoor miles and leads to saddle sores. At this price, you should grab a pair (or two!) before they sell out.

According to recent reports, it’s vital to have a warm, thermal jersey in your closet when the temperature drops. On its own or paired with a light vest, this fleece grid jersey breathes well and keeps you from becoming sweaty and cold. On colder days, wear the Attack Thermal under a windproof jacket to keep your core insulated and cozy.

A test editor favorite for years, Smartwool’s socks are light—but not too light—and have the right amount of compression to keep your feet snug without feeling squeezed. When I find socks I love, I buy a pair every time they go on sale— you can never have too many cycling socks!

For riders who only go full coverage when absolutely necessary, this waterproof cycling cap will be right in their wheelhouse. It offers extra protection from rain, sleet, and wind without added bulk. It’s thin and fits comfortably under a cycling helmet.

If you’re new to winter cycling, you need a thin hat like this one for cold days. It goes under your helmet while keeping your ears and forehead covered. And if you’ve been riding through winters for years, you probably need a new one anyway—that crusty old hat you bought a decade ago has definitely seen better days.

Industry observers note that the CTY 1.1, by REI’s Co-op Cycles house brand, is perfect for commuting, getting around town or campus, or leisurely weekend rides. REI equips the CTY with 40mm-wide, flat-resistant tires, a dependable Shimano 24-speed drivetrain, and disc brakes. The bike is available in five sizes (to fit riders from 5-foot to 6-foot-3) and two colors.

Industry observers note that the Topstone 3 is a perfect entry point into gravel riding. It’s also a great upgrade for riders who need a dependable all-arounder for fitness, commuting, or even bikepacking. The Topstone features a high-quality aluminum frame and a carbon fork, equipped with plenty of mounts for racks, fenders, and bags. For climbing hills, the bike has a Shimano Cues 2x10-speed wide-range drivetrain and easy-to-maintain cable disc brakes for descents. At under $1,400, it’s a great deal for anyone looking for a versatile gravel or all-road bike.

Scott’s Speedster Gravel 30 claims exactly what it is upfront: a speedy gravel bike ideal for racing, group rides, or fast rides on unpaved roads. Sharing design elements with Scott’s more expensive gravel race bikes, the 30 features an aluminum frame, carbon fork, 45mm-wide tires, and a Shimano Cues 1x10 drivetrain with sure-stopping hydraulic disc brakes. The frame uses a UDH hanger, so it’s future-proof if you want to upgrade to a lighterweight groupset once you get addicted to the spirit of gravel.

In a recent development, as Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and New England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.
